speechtext:

5 Copy of order in council of the 17th March, 1908, herewith.
Certified copy of a report of the Committee of the Privy Council, approved by His Excellency the Governor General on the 17th March, 1908.
The Committee of the Privy Council have had under consideration a report, dated 14th March, 1908, from the Minister of the Interior stating that under clause 15 of the regulations approved by order in council of the 6th of February, 1908, respecting the purchase, sale and distribution of grain to homestead settlers in the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan, it is provided that no seed grain shall be supplied to homestead settlers who had sown no crop in the season of 1907. According to the reports received from the officers of the Department of the Interior who have been at work in the west in connection with the distribution, it would appear that the number of applications that are being received for advances of seed grain under the provisions of the regulations is not as large as had been anticipated, and that in consequence that appropriation lately made by parliament to cover this expenditure is likely to be in excess of the requirements.
The minister recommends, inasmuch as numerous applications have been received from farmers in the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan who, although they had sown no crop in 1907, are urgently in need of seed grain during the coming season, and as the machinery for the purchase, distribution and taking of security for advances of seed grain now in operation is well fitted and sufficient to deal with such applications and as the seed grain needed as _ above stated, is uot available in the provinces mentioned, and therefore cannot well be secured by the individual action of those who require it, that clause 15 of the regulations, approved by order in council of the 6th February, 1908, be amended so as to permit of advances to be made to settlers who had sown no crop in the season of 1907,_ under the same terms and conditions as set forth in such regulations.
The Committee submit the same for approval.
(Sgd.) RODOLPIIE BOUDREAU,
Clerk of the Privy Council.

speechtext:
1.	Have the following telegrams been sent by the Department of Justice to Magistrate Palling, of Fort William:
' The Minister of Justice requests that you will be good enough to send immediately report upon case of ten male and nine female Doukhobors committed by you to Port Arthur jail.'

3.	Is it true that they contemplate sending these people to the province of Saskatchewan? If so, on what grounds, under what authority and at whose expense?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: 1. On 14th April inst., the Inspector of Prisons and Public Charities for the pro-
speakername: Hon. A. B. AYLESWORTH (Minister of Justice) :

speechtext:
vince of Ontario and the Inspector of Hospitals and Public Charities for the same province saw me, bringing a letter from the Deputy Attorney General of the province which stated that a number of Doukhobors had come from Saskatoon to Port Arthur, Ontario, and that some of them had been sentenced, for indecent exposure, to the Central Prison and Mercer Reformatory re-pectively. The letter added that there was no room, either at the Central Prison or in the .jail at Port Arthur, and that it was thought the best course would be to have these persons pardoned and let them be removed to the part of the country from which they came where they would be amongst tlielr own people.
The inspectors stated that there were nineteen Doukhobors detained in the jail at Port Arthur and over fifty others living in Fort W7illiam-that all of them, both those at large and those in jail, desired to return to their homes in Saskatchewan, or were willing to do so, but that those who were at large would not go leaving behind those who were in jail, and in these circumstances the inspectors asked that those in jail should be pardoned at once.
I stated that it would be necessary to inquire the views of the convicting magistrate. The inspectors asked me to do so by telegraph and I directed that to be done.
A telegram was accordingly sent in the words following :
April 14, 1908.
Mr. Police Magistrate Palling,
Fort William.
The Minister of Justice requests 'rou will be good enough to send immediately report upon oases of ten male and nine female Doukhobors committed to you to Port Arthur jail.

For Deputy Minister of Justice.
No other telegram or message of any kind relating to the matter was sent by or from the Department of Justice to Mr. Magistrate Palling, or to anybody. I have no knowledge whatever of the other telegram which is quoted in the question put by the hon. gentleman. The newspaper statements that it was sent by me, or from Mr. Power, or any one in the Department of Justice, are entirely without foundation.
The report of the convicting magistrate was received by mail on the 16th April instant, and the case was submitted to His Excellency the Administrator of the government on the 18th instant.
2.	The release of the prisoners has been directed.
3.	It is not true that the government has, or has had, it in contemplation to send these people to the province of Saskatchewan. or to any other place, or to take any step whatever in the matter except to release the nineteen prisoners and leave them at liberty to come or go where they will,

as any other residents of the country might, if the laws of the country are observed.

If a Doukhobor offends against any law, he is in exactly the same position as any other resident of the country who may so offend, and the administration of justice in the province is matter wholly for the authorities of such province.

T notice an item in the Toronto 'Globe' headed ' A Diplomatic Matter ' announcing that Mr. William Mackenzie, one of the press gallery representatives, lias been appointed by the First Minister to establish a new central bureau for handling the correspondence relating to imperial and foreign affairs. The ' Globe ' goes on to say that it will be his duty to keep the correspondence in this connection properly centralized and attended to in an adequate and diplomatic manner. Then it mentions that there are some treaties at present under way, in connection with which Mr. Mackenzie will be found very useful. What are the duties and functions of this diplomat, if I may properly call him so? Is he invested with diplomatic functions? Is this a new office? Will he come under the Civil Service Act? How will his salary be paid? Under what department is he to carry on the work ? At present I understand the foreign correspondence is carried on through the Department of the Secretary of State or the Prime Minister's Department. Are these two to be combined in this new office? Is the work now being done by the Secretary of State and the First Minister to be centered in one individual and under what authority will he come?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: In order to answer more categorically I shall to-morrow lay before the House the order in council which was passed appointing Mr. Mackenzie. In the meantime I may say that he has been appointed a clerk in the office of the Privy Council. His duties will be to classify and keep track of the correspondence, which is now accumulating very fast, from the imperial authorities and colonial and foreign governments. He will have no functions other than those of a clerk and is to be under the orders of the head of tile dexrartment. His salary will be $2,800 per year, which will involve an appropriation of only $800 by this parliament, because the salary of Mr. Foley, who has been promoted to be Clerk of the Crown in Chancery, will be available for that purpose.
I do not ask the question with any view of objecting to the individual, because, so far as I know, he is a suitable man for the position.

I -desire to call the attention of the Minister of Railways to a letter I have received regarding an accident on the Intercolonial Railway between St. Hyacinthe and Quebec, where there have been two accidents lately. The letter is as follows :
I lost a whole day, thanks entirely to the rotten state of the Intercolonial Railway which caused a bad accident to our train, but thanks to a merciful Providence no lives were lost. You ought to bring the matter to the notice of the minister. The line as it is now,

is quite unfit to carry troops or in fact for any heavy traffic. Within two miles of the same place where the run off occurred last Thursday, where the line is perfectly level and so straight that you can see as far as the eye can reach, the weight of the engine caused the spikes in the absolutely rotten ties to give out and let the tender in between the rails. It caught the 90 pound rails and bent them up double. It rolled the baggage car and smashed the baggage and ditched all the rest on their side except the parlour car, which only had the front truck off, and the sleeping car behind. We examined the line carefully and there is no doubt that the accident occurred owing to the rotten ties and want of ballast. The track at that part is in the most disgraceful and unsafe condition.
Is it the intention of the minister to repair the line and has he heard anything about this accident?

speakeroldname: Hon. GEO. P. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways and Canals).
speechtext: I have heard about the accident and very much regret it, but the best conducted railways have their accidents, and as they are somewhat scarce on the Intercolonial Kailway, when one does occur particular attention is drawn to it. The fact is that a part of that portion of the line is considered to have a roadbed equal to any on the continent of America. Just what the particular causes of that accident were I do not know. They are not only being inquired into, but the road has been repaired and the line is running, I presume, as usual. If my hon. friend will give me the name of the individual who has written him, I may he better able to judge the value of his complaint.
When I make any statement in this House I assume the full responsibility, and my name will carry as much weight in this country as that of the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham).

Mr. Speaker, when the House adjourned at six o'clock last evening, I was endeavouring to answer some of the arguments of the bon. member for Stratbcona (Mr. Wilbert McIntyre). I stated then that the arguments brought forward showing the development of the west are not entirely creditable to the system of bonusing immigrants. I stated that a majority of the people in at least a good portion of our western country were American citizens whose entry into our country was easy because of the contiguity of some of the American states to these portions of Alberta and Saskatchewan. I have here an article entitled ' Building a new nation,' and very cleverly written, which seems to corroborate the opinion I enunciated last night. It is a very lengthy article and I have no intention to force it all on the attention of hon. members, but there are certain passages that I desire to read. The author tells of a trip he made in 1901 to that western country and notes the changes which he found in a trip made in 1906. He says:
I travelled westward to the edge of the Rocky mountains and northward in Alberta through plains which, when I first visited them in 1901, wer_e almost peopleless, but which are now thicklv settled and more thoroughly American than the state of New York. I travelled through most of these regions in an immigrant car; talked with some who were seeking new homes, ate with them-in fact, inasmuch as I could, I became an immigrant myself, and tried to look at conditions and the oountry from the viewpoint of the thousands of Americans who are now flocking into the vast fertile regions of the Dominion. . .	[DOT]	[DOT]
I could not have received a more vivid impression of the effects of the so-called ' American invasion of Canada,' than in this comparison of my first trip with my last. Four out of five of the homes that I looked upon were the homes of American farmers; the great majority of the people I met and talked with were Americans. For 1,000 miles westward from Winnipeg along the line of the Canadian Pacific the population of the country and towns to-day is, as I have said, more generally American than is that of the state of New York, and Alberta, especially from the border northward to Edmonton might be regarded as a typical American state.
It goes on to show that the west is so very much Americanized

Will the hon. gentleman (Mr. Robitaille) allow me ? The quotation he has read and his comments upon It would give one the impression that the province of Alberta is more American than the state of New York.
Now it so happens that at the time this party visited the west, in the year 1906, the census of that province was taken. There can be no doubt, therefore, of the exact condition of affairs. The population of Alberta in 1906 was 185.412 people and the number of Americans was 43,251, or 23-3 per cent.
Does the hon. member (Mr. Wilbert McIntyre) admit that there are 400,000 or 500,000 Americans in western Canada who have come in since 1901? The statistics
I can only say that the statistics are incorrect.

What guarantee have I that the hon. gentleman's own figures are more correct than mine? It is a question of good faith. Following the main columns of this army of immigration back to their beginnings, the real reasons of its existence are soon discovered. The momentum is given at the source, and we find men pushing each other up the gangplanks of departing emigrant steamers to make their escape from incredible political and economic wrongs. There is another reason, based upon the first, but none the less potent. The traffic in ocean passages has reached a stage of fierce competition, unscrupulousness and even inhumanity, inconceivable to those not familiar with its details. Men who profit by the march of these millions of people have a drag-net out over continental Europe so fine in its meshes as to let no man, woman or child escape who has the price and the desire or need to go. Several cases of unscrupulousness have been brought to light. This summer, I met two families of French people who had come to Canada via London. One of these people had had some wealth which he had lost in certain mining ventures in Russia and he was coming to Canada to recuperate his lost fortune. He states that whilst in London, the immigration agent

a pretty foxy fellow-succeeded in learning what amount of money he had with him intended for investment in Canada, and, by a series of objections and delays, prevented him from getting on the steamer. The man was practically forced to stay in London for a period of at least three weeks in certain hotels recommended by the immigration men. I do not say these were directly immigration department officials, but booking agents. But it shows that the system affords opportunities for those who try to extract or extort money from intending immigrants on the other side of the water, and that these opportunities have been taken advantage of. It seems to me that it would be well for the government to have a close watch put upon such people through its own immigration officials, and to take every reasonable means to cause the bona fide immigrant to depend upon



tlie immigration offices for information, for booking and even for steamship tickets, rather than leave them in the hands of these men who are but too eager to exploit them in every way. Also, a few days ago, we had what I may call the Doctor Dickey incident concerning which the following appears in a London despatch:
London. March 11.-The trial of Maikeal Lurkis, Charles Harnson and Arshay Atonia, charged with conspiring to defraud emigrants, began at Liverpool yesterday. N. Cockshutt watched the case on behalf of the Canadian government. When Atonia was arrested a large number of letters was found in his possession. Counsel said these letters showed that Atonia was on terms of very intimate relationship with the authorities who had to pass the . emigrants on the other side. One of the letters found on him was from a man who described himself as Hugh L. Dickey, M.D., Halifax. A letter from Halifax, signed W. Dodds, said:
Your eleven people were all passed. Be a little more particular next time with Montreal cases. Do not let them make any signs whatever. If vou describe something that they will wear it will be enough. I felt quite nervous when they all made signs with their hands on their ties.
This clipping shows that the immigration officials do not thoroughly enforce the regulations regarding newcomers when they disembark in Canadian ports. The proof of that is the fact that, in order to procure entry, they have only to put their two hands to their neckties, which is considered a sort of password. It shows further that these men are sent over by unscrupulous partles, probably the booking agents at the other end, in collusion with certain officials of the department who allow these undesirable elements to pass, and if there was no bonus given for each immigrant coming to this country these officials would not be so eager to force immigrants upon us. That bonus is an inducement to fraud and unscrupulousness, and it ought to be condemned on that ground.
Where do our immigrants come from ? From the British isles. London absorbs into her mighty heart thousands of feeble human beings, talking a gibberish of tongues, and quickly becoming public charges. Last year I believe it was stated in this House that there were 1,200 immigration agents in the British isles. The other day certain people took offence at the remarks of my hon. friend from Montmagny (Mr. Armand Lavergne) relative to the Salvation Army. Now I am free to say that the work which the Salvation Army has done in trying to elevate the depressed element of humanity is a most creditable one from a religious standpoint. But when we come to consider the class of people which the Salvation Army deal with we find that men who are broken down financially, men who are demoralized physically, morally and re-Mr. ROB1TAILLE.
iigiously, are brought into the barracks of the Salvation Army who try to do all in their power to make them good citizens. Moreover, we are told that there are certain political evils in England, such as Socialism and collectivism, which imperil the present order of things, not only the monarchy, but also the lords and the ruling classes. Naturally these ruling classes, being the moneyed people, are eager to foster any movement with their advice and patronage, and even with their financial assistance, which will diminish the number of these undesirable classes which the Salvation Army are taking away. The ruling class are all too eager to support the work of tlie Salvation Army in thrusting upon Canada some of the scum of the population. I do not say that all the English immigrants are undesirable, but I am speaking of the work whic-li tlie Salvation Army is doing in taking hold of this low grade of people, and trying to elevate them in the scale of citizenship, and that is the class of people which the Salvation Army is sending over to Canada. We also receive immigrants from continental Europe, particularly from Italy, Austria-Hungary and Russia. These are countries where the majority of people are low in the social scale, and where the percentage of illiteracy is discreditable to the twentieth century. These people are directed to channels of emigration made easy by those seeking cargoes for their ships.
Now, Mr. Speaker, since it has been demonstrated that the bonus system has forced upon us a certain class of undesirable immigrants, what are the consequences that we have to contemplate ? We find first of all an evil effect from a municipal standpoint. The Toronto, Winnipeg and! Montreal newspapers report frequent attacks upon citizens Who are these sinister bandits, and what do they want ? Look up the criminal records, and you will find that 95 per cent of the convicts are penniless immigrants who want to eat, and more especially to drink The charity organizations claim that there are thousands of people who lack the necessities of life. On Bleury street, Montreal, where a charitable institution is located, demands for help are made daily in the shape of food and fuel, In Winnipeg also if we are to believe newspaper reports, there is a large number of penniless and destitute people walking the streets, and armed attacks are made daily upon citizens. In Toronto matters are still worse. The ' Globe.' the ' World,' the * Star,' the ' Mail,' and several other newspapers give us information regarding this class of people. It is not my intention to weary the House with statistics, but It may be well to give a concrete case where a too large number of immigrants have been forced upon the community. Several char-

itable organizations assembled In an extraordinary meeting at Mr. Go Id win Smith's residence, about the beginning of December, 1907, and adopted the following resolution :
1.	That employees of labour are urged, in the name of fraternal spirit, to provide work for the greatest possible number, even if it were necessary to reduce every one's task to a half day's work-
2.	That the municipal authorities are begged to give employment to the greatest possible number even if it is necessary to reduce the dav's work to every one-
3.	That for public works that have not been awarded, the city should exact from the contractors that they employ by day work people of all nationalities-

X may also say that this memorandum, of which I have just given the substance to the House, shows what a burden upon local charities these immigrants have become, and what a tax they are upon citizens from a financial standpoint. I read the other day a very able article in the ' Globe,' covering about the same point I have been elucidating. The title of the article is ' Carefully selected immigrants.' The article deals with the economic aspect of tlie immigration question, and I will take the liberty of quoting a certain portion :
Indeed, the Canadian government have appointed over one hundred employment agents in the agricultural district of the province of Ontario, and are paying them out of public funds for the very purpose of obviating the necessity of a further influx to the large cities of those immigrants who claim that they are going on the land.
That is taken from a letter written by Mr. J. Obed Smith, Assistant Superintendent of Immigration for Canada in Loudon, in reply to a gentleman named Hamilton, of the Church Army, and transmitting to him the new regulations which the government is trying to put into force to prevent the entry into Canada of immigrants thrust upon us by charitable institutions. To give the House an idea of how these people become a charge upon the community I will just glance for a moment at a report prepared by tlie House of Industry of Toronto in which it is stated that they have furnished relief to 2,387 families during last year of whom 484 were recorded as being native-born. If Toronto has to provide for the 222$
relief of 2,387 families bow many others are there who are in need, but who have not made applicaion for assistance ? The report continues:
Despite the large arrivals of immigrants from southern Europe, comparatively few of them applied for assistance.
Another point that I wish to call the attention of the House to is one that has been brought forward by the hon. member lor Jacques Cartier, and it is one in regard to which the lion. Minister of the Interior has not given any answer. How can the government explain that from 1901 to 190C the settlers reported by the department as having been located in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta are 200,000 to 250,000 short of the number which the immigration returns are supposed to have shown? That is a point that the minister has not touched.
Now, I wish to call the attention of the House to the objection which can be raised to this forced immigration system from the provincial standpoint. The immigration policy, as carried out by this government, results in increasing the population of the western provinces and in enhancing tlie value of land retained by the railway companies as well as by companies of tlie stamp of the Saskatchewan Valley Land company. it also increases tlie population of tlie province of Ontario who are supposed to take care of immigrants as soon as they arrive in the country and try to establish them on farms or secure positions for them in other walks of life. In Quebec, only a few years ago, we succeeded in getting one single agent appointed who was supposed, not to work for Quebec, but to try to augment the population of the eastern townships. I shall refer, at greater length to this gentleman in a few moments. I do not enunciate this opinion in any unwarranted manner. A few days ago my bon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) enquired of the government to what religious denominations different people holding offices under the government belonged. If we could rely on our English friends generally sharing the sentiment which was expressed in reply to that question by the lion. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) we, in Quebec, would entertain no fears that our prestige would suffer as a result of the policy of the immigration branch of the Department of the Interior. The idea of the preponderance of any one race in Canada is contrary to the spirit of the constitution which was framed for the purpose of maintaining the equilibrium between the different races inhabiting this country. Tlie question is brought up. not in a spirit of aggressiveness, but as a matter of self-defence, and it is a result of such racial appeals as that to which I shall now call tlie attention of the House. The Hon. Mr. Weir, who happens to hold an official position in tlie local government of Quebec,

speaking on the 18th July, 1907, before a Protestant synod, described the English depopulation of the province of Quebec as a national peril and suggested the establishment of an organization which would prevent rural property from passing out of English hands, Protestant ministers would, he said, advise this organization of the departure of an English farmer in order that he might be replaced by one of the same nationality. This could only be effected by immigration. Why not, Mr. Weir asked, direct towards the province of Quebec, a portion of that large English immigration wave bound for the west. What was the effect of this speech? The first practical result of this suggested policy for the English population of the eastern townships was the nomination of Mr. E. W. Brewster, the only immigration agent who performs duties corresponding to those of the 199 agents in Ontario. That shows you how fairly Quebec has been treated on this immigration question. When we pay 40 per cent of the money that the government collect in revenue we ought, at least, to get our fair share of the expenditure not only in public works but with regard to this question of immigration the object of which, according to certain officials, seems to be to maintain the preponderance of one nationality. One and a half years' work by Mr. Brewster resulted in the location of about 1,500 immigrants in the eastern part of the province of Quebec, known as the eastern townships. That is the figure as given by the Minister of the Interior on April 15. 1907, in answer to an inquiry. The basic policy is to strengthen the British element. This policy has already borne its fruit in as much as within the space of one year it has added 16 English ridings to confederation. In fifteen years we, of the province of Quebec, shall form one-tenth of the whole population of this country; in twenty years this policy if carried out, will have caused the placing of 1,000,000 English immigrants in the northern part of Quebec, and in twenty-five years the English element will have conquered the eastern townships. Our premier himself sees no difficulty in admitting that in a quarter of a century Canada will have a population of 30,000,000. Sandwiched between the English of the far west, the English of the eastern provinces, between the Americans massed to the south of us and the English established in the north all along the Transcontinental route what influence will we have on the destinies of the nation? They say that an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure. Let us put this into practice. Now is the time to act. To-morrow it may be too late. What effect has this undesirable immigration upon us from a national standpoint? It will be necessary to notice the influence of immigration on the growth of population and to follow the ethnic changes which are being, wrought thereby. Equally important Mr. ROBITATLLE.
is it to observe the effect of immigration on the economic condition of the labouring classes in this country, whether it is made better or worse. In the same way it is advisable to study the influence of the newcomers on the ethical consciousness of the community, whether there is a gain or a loss to us. In short, we must set up our standard of what we desire this nation to be and then consider whether the policy we hitherto pursued in regard to immigration is calculated to maintain that standard or to endanger it. As to the character of the immigration I shall quote expressions of opinion from prominent Canadians, men who hold high position in the land and who can impartially view this question. I quote from Judge McMahon, who believes in securing immigrants that will be a credit to the country.
Mr. Justice McMahon, at the opening of the spring assizes yesterday, expressed his satisfaction that the duties of the grand iury would not he unusually onerous. But there was one matter which he brought to the jurymen's attention.
Dr. Clarice, superintendent of Toronto asylum, the judge said, stated recently :	' Of
362 admissions of lunatics last year 136 were foreign born, the majority recent arrivals. Those that the province will never get rid of amount to about 40. Each patient retained will cost the province $G.000.'
Sixty-five per cent of these weak-minded foreigners were afflicted with dementia proe-cox, the same form of insanity accredited to Harry K. Thaw. They were the failures sent from the old country by immigration companies to try and make good in Canada.'
The judge stated that the disease was usually contracted in early life and that 60 per cent of the cases became evident before the age of 25 years. 'We pay for immigration; then why not secure those who will be a credit to the country rather than a detriment to its progress ? '
Here is another quotation from a newspaper :
M. Regimbal, assistant agent of immigration for the district of Montreal, left for Portland last evening having in his charge 21 English immigrants who came from the west and who are to be deported. One of these is a lunatic, and the others have refused to do any work, and so are sent back to their country.
I do not mean to have it inferred by these quotations that by any means the entire immigration from England is undesirable, but I read them simply as a basis for my statement that no matter from what country people come they should be of a class calculated to advance the interests of Canada. I quote from Mr. Justice Lavergne who was at one time a law partner of the right lion, the Prime Minister, and who said :
For the last vear or so crime seems to have become epidemic among Italians of the lower classes. Men with the worst of records in

the old country invade out shores and lead here a life of crime.
Mr. Bruce Smith, inspector of prisons for Ontario, in his last annual report to the government, says :
Although the year closes with the largest number that have been in confinement in the jails of Ontario within the past twenty years, this increase is not due to any increase in crime in the province, but is largely due to Canada, and especially Ontario, being made the dumping ground during the past year of some most, undesirable immigrants. Every jail I have visited within the past six months has had among its prisoners persons who have been only a few months in this country. Some of them have spent most of their lives in English prisons. Several have admitted that they had been discharged by English magistrates on condition that they would emigrate to Canada. There must be something radically wrong with our immigration regulations that will permit such apparent neglect in the inspection of persons seeking and obtaining passage as immigrants to this country. The whole system of encouraging such people to seek a home in Canada is wrong, and the sooner the conditions complained of are recognized and changed the better.
These statements from men who are in a position to know show that undesirable immigrants are coming to our shores and that for the sake of gaining a few paltry dollars the immigrant agents are sending them here.
Let us look at this question from the economic standpoint. Economic well-being is a difficult thing for a nation to acquire, aud once acquired is too precious to give up without a struggle-once lost it may require generations to attain again even if the economic conditions are favourable. The standard of living in this country should be jealously guarded, so that our working classes should not either consciously or unconsciously lose it. It may be lowered in either of two ways. Excessive immigration may overstock the labour market and reduce wages ; or immigrants accustomed to fewer of the comforts of life may supplant the native workman. In either ease we have brought undue pressure to bear on the mass of the people and have forced them down to a lower level. We have substituted the lower for the higher and preferred that which is inferior. On this point I quote the following from the Toronto ' Globe ' of April the 17th :
If there is a great demand for men in Toronto when the seductive steamship agent is talking to the intending emigrant in London, it is no assurance that there will be any demand when the same emigrant reaches this city. Such instances go to show how widely the impression has been spread abroad and accepted that Canada is a country in which the laws of political economy have no existence.
Now, let us look at the question from the electoral standpoint. The continued addition to our electorate of hundreds of thousands of persons who have had no training in self-government, who have other and quite different state of action-will this not tend to weaken our political capacity and self-reliance ? Will it not also effect the adjustment of our institutions to our people. an adjustment which is so necessary if the institutions are to work successfully ?
If the new beam of our political life have neither the aspirations which our ancestors cherished, nor the experience which we have cherished, will not the homogeneousness of our social organizations he seriously imperilled ? A free ballot which was safe in the hands of our intelligent and self-respecting democracy is no longer safe in those of an ignorant and degraded proletariat. Will these alien races rule at the ballot box ? Will they govern our great cities ? What will be their rule ? Will their be the dominant church life ? What will he their faith ? Will their children determine our social and industrial conditions ? What will be their ideals and standards ? We must answer for all this. These immigrants are our raw material out of which we make our to-morrow. Canada welcomes the self-supporting, intelligent and healthy foreigners ; but unfortunately for the peace aud safety of well governed communities in this promising country of ours, a very large proportion of these now on the move cannot, even by courtesy or true sympathy, be placed under this classification. Patriotism, loyalty and other civic virtues are by the present immigration policy sinking to a low ebb. In conclusion, Mr. Speaker. I am pleased to support the motion of my hon. friend (Mr. Monk)-1. Because the premiums are paid to other parties than for those intended by the regulations ; 2. Because a bonus incites greed of graft and thereby has forced upon us undesirable immigrants which inevitably shall lower our standard of ideals. To these immigrants I would apply the words of the poet :
Canada, charge not thv fate to these;
The power is ours to mold them or to mar,
But freedom's voice, far down the centuries.
Shall sound our choice from blazing star to star.

Mr. Speaker, I have very much pleasure in supporting the resolution which has been brought forward by the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk). The question of immigration is one that is attracting and should receive more attention from this House and this country than probably any other question that can be discussed. When this House met in November last I took the

earliest opportunity of placing on the Order Paper a resolution dealing with this very matter. As that resolution has not been and probably will not be again reached, I take this opportunity of making the few remarks which I otherwise would have made in closing the debate on that resolution.
The hon. Minister of the Interior the other day made the broad statement that there were ten men out of work in 1896 to one who is out of work in 1908 ; I think those were about his words. So far as my observation goes, if he had reversed that statement and said that there were ten out of work to-day for every one who was out of work in 1896, he would have been mucli nearer the mark. I think every hon. member of this House who has anything to do with labour will corroborate my statement. I deplore the fact of the hon. minister sending out broadcast the statement he made, when everybody knows that there are hundreds and thousands without employment in our towns and cities to day. I have been found fault with because I have drawn attention to this state of affairs. There are two ways of meeting a difficulty : one is to say that it does not exist; the other is to recognize it and endeavour to get a remedy for it. I have taken the latter course, but the hon. minister says no difficulty exists. It is true, the hon. Minister of the Interior and the hon. member for Strathcona (Mr. Wilbert McIntyre) say that we are quite out of touch with western conditions, and that the immigration policy must entirely hinge on what the west wants. I think we might retort that these hon. gentlemen know very little about the requirements of the east if they make the statement that there is room in this country for many others seeking employment, and requiring to get work almost the day they land. The Minister of the Interior makes the statement that the bonus is doing a public good and has been adopted in order that we might have a selected class of immigrants. i do not find that it works that way at all. I think the minister, long before he became a minister, took the ground that the bonus was the means of bringing in those who were not desirable. That statement was made yesterday, and I did not hear the minister contradict it. Whether that is the case or not, in my opinion the offering of a bonus for immigrants is the most approved way of getting an undesirable class. There are other weaknesses in the immigration policy of the government, but none so great as the bonus. See how it works. A man who may be dissatisfied with his position in the country to which he owes his birth, or who may be out of work, 'makes up his mind to go abroad. He goes to a ticket office to make inquiries with regard to South Africa, Australia, the Argentine Republic, the West Indies or some other country, many or all Mr. COCKSHUTT
of which are not offering a bonus at all. But the ticket agent, knowing that a bonus is offered by the Canadian government, at once sees an opportunity of turning an honest five dollars, and he endeavours to persuade the immigrant that Canada is the country to go to. The man may have felt that Canada was unsuitable for him, on account of climate or for some other reason, but he is deflected from the course he had intended to take by the ticket agent, and is induced to come to Canada. The minister will say : ' That is good policy ; I approve of that ; we are getting lots of people.' There are many other things to be taken into account in order to judge whether this great influx of immigrants is a public advantage. I can easily conceive of a situation in which a large immigration is a source of weakness rather than a source of strength especially if a large proportion of those we are getting belong to an undesirable class ; and that we are getting many of that class goes without saying-the fact is too well known. The hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Robitaille) has read a long list of pronouncements by judges and others. These men are not biassed, and yet they point out that we are receiving large numbers of the undesirable class, which is largely attributable to the bonus system.
I notice that some Liberal papers are taking the ground that people who oppose the bonus system do so because they do not understand it, they being under the impression that the immigrant gets the bonus, and not the booking agent. I think very few indeed are under that impression. That is simply drawing a red herring across the track. There might be a good deal said in favour of the poor immigrant getting the five dollars, because it would help him to pay his way for a little while after he lands in this country. But it is the booking agent who gets the five dollars. Though we are paying' hundreds of thousands of dollars every year in this way, the money is a small matter compared with the wrong done to the country in getting here so many of the undesirable class-people who are not able to maintain themselves on the soil after they get here.
I was much interested and to some extent pleased with the speech which my hon. friend from South Perth (Mr. G, H. McIntyre) delivered in this House yesterday. We have several members of this House who may be said to be independent members. Their independence is not always evident; yet on this occasion we have had three of the so-called independent members speaking, and all of them have condemned the bonus system. But our hon. friend from South Perth, who I am sorry to see is not in the House at the present time, delivered a long oration on this question. When that hon. gentleman was elected he

posed as an independent; but of all the questionable policies that he could very well have called in question, he went so far as to endorse the bonus system as at present carried on by this government, although he said that the day was near at hand when it must go. In my opinion, Sir. Speaker, the bonus system has been retained very much too long. If there ever was any excuse for it, that time has long since passed away. It should have been abolished years ago. The hon. member for South Perth put the Minister of the Interior away up on a pedestal. He said that he stood as the one man who had more to say about what Canada was and what it should be in the future than any other man in the Dominion of Canada.
1 am not willing to place the minister on quite so high a pedestal. I hold him responsible to a certain extent for this policy, but it is the government, which is paying out the money to enable him to carry out that policy, that the people will hold responsible. The hon. gentleman told us that we require people in this country and are not afraid to pay for them. He says that the west is badly in need of people and that the bonus system is approved of by the large majority of our population. Well, I have been in the west two or three times recently but did not have an opportunity of discussing the bonus question at any great length with our friends there; but I can speak for the province of Ontario, with which I am familiar, and I am satisfied that if to-day a plebiscite were taken in that province as to whether or not a bonus should be paid for immigrants from any country in Europe, 75 per cent would say no. And what I say with regard to Ontario, I believe, would apply with almost equal force to Quebec and the maritime provinces. I do not believe that the west would be unanimous on this question, but admitting that 50 per cent would be in favour of continuing the bonus system, if you take the whole country through you will find that 75 per cent of our people, if asked by a plebiscite, would say that we should pay no more bonuses for immigrants. Why should we? We have the best country under the sun. We give 100 acres of No. 1 land to every man who will take up a homestead. We have the freest and best institutions of any country almost under the sun and a country with a climate and opportunities second to none. Why then should we go beyond these natural re-soui-ces? After we have given a man 100 acres of land, after we have offered him all this country has to give, why should we pay $5 a head to a booking agent to send him here? Is there any good reason for our doing this especially when the United States is charging 84 per head on immigrants going into that country? The Americans charge $4 a head for permission to enter the United States, and we pay $5 per
head to get people to come to Canada, making a difference of $9 between the two countries. And besides we have more to offer intending settlers than has the United States. Let me point out a danger which is menacing, and which I have not heard any one discussing. According to the American papers there are between 4,500,000 and
5.000.	000 people in the towns and cities of the United States to-day without employment. Those people are in many instances within twenty-four hours of our border and can cross at any moment. That is a fact which should receive the serious attention of the government. We are too close to our neighbours in the south not to feel every breeze that blows on them. When financial conditions are bad there, they are bad here, when the labour market is not good there it is not good here. Today there are in the United States between
4.000.	000 and 5,000,000 people who are walking in the streets without anything to do. That is a serious problem. It is one which should cause us to pause in our policy of paying men to come to this country, who have no profession and in many instances are undesirable.
The hon. minister said that we had the right to deport undesirable immigrants within two years. If any municipality lias undesirable citizens all it had to do was to deport them. But that must be done within two years of their arrival, and the minister throw's the burden of doing it on the . municipalities. The government brings them in at $5 per head and then unloads them on the municipalities and saddles on the municipalities the whole onus of the transaction. Why should the onus be thrown on the municipalities? If any deporting is to be done, it should be done by the government w'hic'h brought in these undesirables and not saddle that expense on the municipalities. Let me point out the attitude of the government with regard to the Doukhobors, we have heard so much about. We had a long discussion the other day about the invasion of Ontario by these Doukhobors from the Northwest Territories. The Minister of the Interior then told ns that these people could not be deported because they had been here eight years and were free citizens of Canada. Under that ruling of the Minister of the Interior, confirmed by the Minister of Justice, there is no man under the sun who could not come Into this country and free himself from the risk of deportation. On landing he could go to some of the unsettled districts in the north, and w7e have lots of such districts in Ontario and Quebec and the other provinces. He could, as the Doukhobors did, settle outside the pale of civilization and remain there until the two years w'ere up. That is what the Doukhobors did, and now we have them marching back into the heart of the country, and the Minister of Justice

said that those men have been given the freedom of the country and can come and go as they please the same as any other citizen in Canada. But we are told by the Minister of the Interior that we are all equally responsible for their coming. Well, I do not hold myself in the slightest degree responsible, and there are dozens of others in this House who can equally say that they cannot be held responsible. We were not in this House ten years ago when the immigration of these Doukhobors was started: and no man who has been elected to this House since that time can be charged with any responsibility in this matter. These people were brought out at heavy cost. It cost the country $7.50 per head' to bring them here, and if we could get rid of them at $50 a head we would be doing a great stroke of business in the interests of this country. But the Minister of the Interior says that they have been here eight years and are consequently free to go or stay as they like. I refer to this in order to show that, under our deportation law, we have no control over these people. Undesirable people may come into tins country and settle in the northern, part of Ontario and after they have been there two years, they are free to settle in any of our towns or cities or in any other centre of population in this country they please. If they went immediately to any city in Ontario, they would no doubt be deported at once. But they do not. What they are advised to do is to go into some remote district and remain there two years. Then they have perfect freedom to come and go and violate by their eccentricities the decencies of life, and there is no means by which we can rid ourselves of them. This government boasts of the great things it has done. Well, this country has not yet fully realized what this government has done with regard to immigration. They have inflicted on us a burden that it will take the toil and the strain of one to two generations to remove.
The hon. member for South Perth (Mr. G. H. McIntyre), who spoke very feelingly and very properly with regard to immigration in the old days, touched a theme he might very well have enlarged upon. Look at the immigration that flowed into the provinces of Ontario and Quebec when this country was being settled. Go back a hundred years when this territory in the midst of which we assemble was one vast wilderness. There came into this province and the province adjoining it a little band of sturdy citizens driven out of Great Britain by the stern law of famine. No bonus was paid to these men to come here. They came here and hewed out their homes in what were then the wilds. They settled in the forest and for forty or fifty years they lived almost shut out from civilization and humanity, but all the time hewing out places for themselves and building strong 1 Mr. COCKSHUTT.
and true the foundations of the citizenship that we have enjoyed for fifty years. We owe to these people a debt of gratitude we never can repay. But we can show that at least we feel the gratitude we would like to express by preserving unsullied and undimmed the citizenship they banded down to us when they passed to their reward. But are we doing that under the policy of this government ? I think not. We have thrown all that to the winds ; we have no regard for it to-day but we are going on simply looking to numbers, as the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver) has stated-it is simply a matter of numbers to be brought in regardless of whether their coming will or will not be a lasting good to the country.
With regard to that particular point I wish to draw attention to the fact that the older provinces of Canada have been, thus far. mainly responsible for the settlement of the west. That is a statement that, I believe, neither the Minister of the Interior nor any other hon. gentleman on that side will gainsay-that the large proportion of the settlement of the West has been effected from the provinces of Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. Probably 50 per cent of the people in the West to-day are Canadian by birth. I have not the figures at hand, but I know that, at least, within recent times, that proportion would hold good. These people have been drawn from the older provinces very largely within the last ten years and so great has been the drain upon us, especially upon our farming community, that we have parted with almost every farmer's son that the older provinces could possibly spare- I fear far more than they should have spared-and to-day we have in the older provinces scarcely enough men to man our own farms. I am pointing this out to show that this element that has gone from the older provinces and that has become the backbone of the Northwest has been drawn upon to its limits-we can go no further ; we have not the men to spare. The older provinces can no longer afford the population necessary to assimilate the incoming hordes of Europe. If that be the case, are we nevertheless to go on receiving a great immigration from Europe without mixing with it the representative Canadian citizenship to make these people good citizens ? The colonization of any part of the West by a particular nation is bound to be a failure. It has always been a failure in every sense of the word. We must have only one citizenship in the Dominion of Canada, and that the citizenship of broad Can-adianism ; but this we can never have if we are going to keep together in one settlement the immigrants coming from any section of Europe, whether they be Doukhobors or any other. They will never get over the evils that they have brought in. The only way is to have population go in

tliat will spread out to all tlie provinces of Canada and that will become Canadian in the broad sense.
Mow, I have said that this is not a matter simply of the growth of the country, nor of the labour of the country. But I would point out that organized labour, I believe, without any exception, is utterly opposed to the bonus system. The hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Verville), who spoke the other day upon this question, the hon. member for Montinagny (Mr. Armand Lavergne) and the hon. member for Quebec County (Mr. Robitaille), representing as they do, large elements of labour, have all been against it. We know that almost every trade and labour council in Canada has passed resolutions opposing the proposition of this government to pay further bonuses. . In considering this matter. we must not neglect the interests of labour for they are a factor of our population of which we should take the greatest care. They have been in this country many of them all their lives and others for many years. Is it right or just to bring in from the countries of Europe a lower class of citizenship to displace and supplant the men who, with their wives and families, are dependent upon getting work in the places in which they have lived so long ? The common cause of humanity would declare this unjust and say that it should immediately cease. The Minister of the Interior seems to have the idea that he can force prosperity in this country by bringing in a vast influx of people. I take the opposite view. I say that if we have a stringency to-day or if our trade is at all depressed at this time, that stringency and that depression can be materially increased and the burdens of the people multiplied by bringing in more people, who, instead of being a help at this time will become an encumbrance and will add still further to our difficulties by their calls for charity. But this is what we have seen in Ontario. Yet the Minister of the Interior has the hardihood to rise in his place and tell us that there were ten men out of work in 1896 for one man out of work to-day. The hon. gentleman was entirely astray in his facts. There is no doubt' that this bonus question is receiving, as it should, the very earnest attention of the citizens of the Dominion of Canada. And our hon. friends opposite seem to be disposed to continue this policy. If I were looking at this from a political point of view, I should not find fault with their taking that course, because the more they advocate this policy the worse will they stand in the opinion of the country. I could ask no better campaign literature than reprints of their arguments in support of this policy. I could ask no better campaign speech in favour of my election than to have the hon. member for South Perth (Mr. G. H. McIntyre) come down to Brantford and advocate the bonus
system as carried on by this government. I would welcome the hon. gentleman as a worker in my interest. Nothing could be more detrimental to the interests of the government in the towns and cities of the Dominion than the continuation of this bonus on immigrants coining to this country. You may say :	' Why give away
your tricks ? ' It is bad politics I admit. But the minister has charged me with keeping politics in view in everything I do. I admit that what I am doing is bad politics, but I feel compelled, in the interests of Canada, to declare that the government is pursuing a suicidal policy in regard to immigration. This system should have been stopped not this year merely but several years ago. There may have been a time when it was safe, when the immigration brought in was a negligible quantity as the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) has said. But that time has gone by. pur immigration has increased by leaps and bounds. And we need not fear that it will unduly decrease. This country is so well known, its resources have been so widely advertised, its capability of producing a living for additional millions of people is so widely appreciated, that it should not require a single dollar, either for advertising or for bonuses, to bring into Canada every man who can possibly be employed or planted upon the soil to advantage.
Take the history of the United States, our great neighbours to tlie south, and you will find the same facts I have pointed out with regard to Canada. Two or three hundred years ago that country was almost unknown. Look at the class of men that come out in those days and planted the flag, and started in to hew out a home in the wilderness where they could worship God according to the dictates of their own conscience. That little band, under the providence of God, multiplied and increased until it was able to furnish a leaven that has made a nation to the south of us second to none, in intelligence and civilization, on the face of the earth. We have to some extent in the older provinces of Canada a like leaven that we seem disposed to part with very lightly. We cannot assimilate all the people that these gentlemen wish to bring in to the extent they have been bringing them in, without doing great injustice to Canada. I say it, and I feel it, Mr. Speaker, that we have to-day within the confines of this Dominion all the people of the classes that have been coming in lately, that can possibly be taken care of and given a good home, and become good citizens in the territory where they have chosen to settle. Tours very truly,

My hon. friend who, one or two years ago, was advocating a stimulation of Immigration to this country, forgot that it was utterly impossible to carry on a national policy of immigration for any length of time without such immigration receiving a momentum that it would be impossible to stop all at once. The farmers of Ontario, I believe, are in a very prosperous condition. They are suffering more perhaps, from lack of help upon the farm than from any other one cause. That I know is the main factor in our part of Ontario. I think it is the duty of the immigration department-

-while they are bringing out the vast number of stalwart men from the old country that they do, to see to it that Old Ontario is not entirely passed by. It was in this way that my hon. friend declaimed in this House a year ago. -and so the farmer is without help and has not been able to take advantage of the prices that are going so much as he would have done if he had been able to hire others to help him produce large quantities of goods.
