The minister has put a question to me and I think I should have the privilege of answering it.

Perhaps the House will give me three or four minutes as I am obliged to go to a meeting this evening. I want to say to my hon. friend that there is no citizen of Canada who has not an equal opportunity with every immigrant to take up land in the Northwest.
I deny that.
Well, my hon. friend is afraid to allow me to give him his answer. I do not make statements without being prepared to vindicate them.
Six o'clock.

My hon. friend asks: How is it that immigrants from the British isles can go to the Northwest at a less rate than people from Quebec? The government have nothing to do with that; they do not determine the rate.
What about the railway commission?
Has my hon. friend submitted that grievance to the railway commission?
Is it not the duty of the Minister of the Interior to submit it to the railway commission?
Six o'clock.

I cannot conclude before six o'clock, and I must thank the House for their consideration. Will hon. members give me one minute? I want to say a word to the House and to the government. What the people of this country want is a bold and courageous government which will get settlers unto the lands. There may be weaknesses and mistakes in some cases, because the government is made up of human beings, just like other poor creatures, there are no such things as cabi-

nets of angels in this country any more than in any other, hut I want to say that the people are looking to the Laurier government to promote, even more extensively than they are doing to-day, the development of this great country by the extension of the principle that they have adopted in applying strict regulations to immigration on this side of the line and in granting financial and other assistance that discretion and supervision may be exercised on the other side of the line in favour of bona fide settlers to the end that these people may be placed upon the land, that more markets and greater opportunities may be opened up and that the country may be further developed as a consequence of this policy. I want to assure my right lion, friend that in spite of everything that has been said the great mass of the people will support this policy and forgive a whole lot of the small trifles that lion, gentlemen put before the country and waste time iu discussing in this House. These are small matters that never reach the corridors of this House, but the great development of this magnificent country and the placing of settlers with a Crown title on the public lands, to bold them for ever for the benefit of themselves and their families, to live under our institutions and to be the subjects of a free British government, is the natural result of the policy which this government have adopted and I want to say that is the policy that will be supported by the people. The government wants to go ahead. Do not take any notice of these whinings and complainings. This whole debate has been one funeral dirge as if the country were going to the devil. We are getting into a terrible condition when some man in Liverpool is getting $10 for sending a man to this country which will enrich it to the extent of hundreds of dollars, or when some other individuals in some other countries are getting a few dollars for sending people here who will enrich Canada to the extent of thousands of dollars. The people understand this policy and they will support it. There is nothing in the position taken by bon. gentlemen opposite. If the government exercise close supervision and make a selection of suitable immigrants their coming will be a great benefit to this country as land settlers.
At six o'clock, House took recess.
After Recess.
House resumed at eight o'clock.

The hon. gentleman from Nanaimo (Mr. Ralph Smith), enunciated the view, so far as I could hear his closing remarks, that many of the attacks made on the government by the Conservative opposition would not penetrate beyond the corridors of this House. If the volume of his voice was the
measure of how far the hon. gentleman's speech would carry, his utterances would certainly get beyond the precincts of this building, but I venture to think that when the hon. gentleman (Mr. Ralph Smith) has time to reflect he will be glad if some of his statements in the latter part of his speech should remain in oblivion to those whom he mainly represents in this House. The hon. gentleman made a new departure this afternoon and although he had volume of voice he had not the volume of independence we would expect from him. The hon. gentleman has seen' fit for reasons best known to himself to turn his back upon the labour party which he was supposed to champion, and to stand on both feet for the government party in support of their immigration policy. I do not propose to follow my hon. friend in his dealings with the labour party, because no doubt they will themselves determine how far they are satisfied with him. However, if you give certain people rope enough they will hang themselves, and that seems to be the misfortune of the hon. gentleman. He asked for more time to finish his speech, and then with the assistance of the Minister of the Interior he endeavoured to crowd down the statement of the member for Montmagny that in the matter of transportation, there was discrimination between immigrants coming to this country, and our own good citizens. A moment's reflection will show that there is a distinct discrimination against the people of Canada in the matter of transportation. If the sons of the province of Quebec for example, wish to go to the west they are not carried by the transportation companies upon the same terms as the poorest and most wretched foreigners who come to our shores.
Does the hon. gentleman think that the policy of the government should be to transplant the people of this country from one portion of it to another 1

When hon. gentlemen on the other side interrupt me to ask a question that has no relevancy to the point I am discussing I do not propose to answer. The question of the hon. gentleman has absolutely no relation to the matter with which I am dealing. The hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Ralph Smith) thought tit to deliver a vicious attack upon the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt), and if the hon. gentleman (Mr. Cockshutt) had the privilege of replying I would not refer to it for I know he could dispose of the hon. member for Nanaimo in good style. He attacked the member for Brantford because, he said, he has changed his views on this question since May of 1903. But what ground is there for condemnation. The hon. member (Mr. Ralph Smith) alleges that

at that time the hon. member for Brantford advocated the importation of skilled labour Into Brantford and other cities of the Dominion. I do not admit that such a position was ever taken by the hon. member for Brantford.
It was.

I prefer to take the documents rather than the statement of my hon. friend from Cape Breton with respect to that. And the written evidence shows that what the member for Brantford did was to forward to the proper department a letter from one of his constituents.
And what did he ask ?
Never mind for the present ; you are very fond of breaking in.
I thought you would not answer.

The hon. member for Nanaimo has condemned the hon. member for Brantford because he alleges that in May, 1905, that hon. gentleman advocated the immigration into this country of skilled labour, and that now he has changed his attitude in regard to that. Would the hon. member for Nanaimo dare to take the position to-day that he advocates the introduction of skilled labour into Canada ? He did take a pretty distinct departure from the position of an advocate of the labour party ; but he would not dare to take the position that he advocates the indiscriminate immi-? ation into this country of skilled labour and artisans ; and yet, with his inconsistency, he attempts to condemn the hon. member for Brantford.
Again, he condemns the hon. member for Brantford because he says that a year ago that hon. member advocated immigration into this country, whereas to-day he says he condemns immigration into this country. The hon. member for Nanaimo has not properly sized up the situation. I venture to say that neither he nor any other member of this House can find, in all the speeches made by hon. members on this side, during either this or preceding debates on immigration, one utterance condemning immigration to this country. It is not immigration that we condemn, but it is the system which he government pursues of bonusing booking agents to send to this country a class of immigrants that we do not want.
The hon. member for Nanaimo waxed eloquent over the position he takes on the question of religion in connection with the class of immigrants he desires to see brought into this country. Now, I do not for a moment say that we are to make nice distinctions in this regal'd as to the class of people who come to this country; but when I find the hon. gentleman stating that he does not care whether an immigrant is an Mr. LENNOX.
atheist or a Christian, that the moral or religious attitude of the immigrant is an entirely immaterial question to him, I venture to say that the good sense of the people of this country will not join with the hon. member in that position. Speaking for myself, while I draw no narrow lines in this regard, holding that a man can exercise his conscience in the way he sees fit, I do feel that it is important that we shall bring into this country a class who shall be God-fearing people, and that it shall not go forth that an atheist is an acceptable citizen of this country. What is atheism? It is the absolute repudiation of the existence of God ; and do you want it to go forth that the representatives of the people in this parliament have got to the position that they care not at all whether the class of immigrants who come into this country are or are not such as the hon. gentleman said he was quite willing to have come into the country-atheists and men of that class ? I am sorry the hon. gentleman is not here, but I strongly commend tQ the perusal of the labour party in this country the utterances of that hon. gentleman this afternoon. I think it will be a surprise to them to find that he has so utterly and completely abandoned them and gone over, as I could have predicted long ago he would, holus bolus to the present administration.
Now, I have never spoken upon the question of immigration, although I have thought very seriously upon it ever since I came into this House. I have been somewhat puzzled as to the best policy to pursue having regard to a certain class of the inhabitants of this country. I have always felt that the people whose interests should be most anxiously considered are the people who form the backbone of this country, the farmers; and from a careful watching of this debate, I think I can say without any fear of contradiction that not one note has been sounded from the government side in favour of the agriculturists of this country. I believe that whilst we should endeavour to advance the interests of all classes, the interests of the bulk of the communitv. of those who contribute most to the country's progress and prosperity are most to be considered. The farmers are the largest class in the country, and if I were convinced that a payment of money, by bonuses or otherwise, for the purpose of promoting immigration would be in their interest in the sense of giving them the labour they require on their farms, I would not be prepared to condemn it in any way. But I am convinced, from a careful observance of the policy of the government, that we shall never get in this country a class that are required to labour on the farms of Ontario and the other older provinces, or for assistance to the farmers who are settled in the west, by the system we are pursuing at the present time. Now,

as to the relative position of the farmers and another great class in this country, the manufacturers, we have in Canada farmers, owners and tenants, to the number of 544,688. Computing in the ordinary way the residents on the farm, the people who are dependent directly on agriculture for their existence, will number 2,723,440, or more than 50 per cent of the entire population of Canada. From the census returns of 1901, T find that the farmers have invested in their farms and implements and various means of carrying on their indus-trv $1,787,102,620. and that they pay for hired help $24,173,988 annually. On the other hand, the investments of the manufacturers amount to $446,916,487. Of this their working capital, which can hardly be called a permanent investment, amounts to $237,537,849, leaving only a little over $200.000,000 as an actual permanent investment by the manufacturers of the country. The farmers therefore have at stake as a permanent investment in this country, in order to advance its prosperity, four times as much as all the manufacturers of the country. Then, take the products. The farmers of Canada in 1901-and there has been a vast increase since then-produced $363,126,384, whereas the manufacturers, if we take the sales, produced $481,053,375. But the amount of raw material which went into the manufactured products and a large portion of which was produced on the farm was $266,527,858. Therefore the actual product of the manufacturers was $215,525,517, as compared with the figures I have given with reference to the farm. In other words, the products of the farm exceed the products of the factories some 70 per cent. What I say is this. We must not neglect the interests of any class, but all the same we should keep steadily in view the fact that Canada is preeminently a great farming country. The farming interests should therefore be the first consideration of any competent and wise government because that which is the greatest producer must tend in the greatest degree to the prosperity of the country.
I know that the policy of the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver) is a western policy and a western policy alone. I do not object to a western policy within proper limits. It is a policy to people the farm lands of the west. But we want something more than that. Our first object should be to secure farm help. Labour is wanted on the farms of Canada, and if we do not see to it, the finest land in any part of the world to-day-I refer particularly to the older portions of Canada-will be left uncultivated for the lack of an adequate labour supply. Therefore the first consideration of the government should be, not so much to get farmers to take up farms in the west, as to get in farm help. Get in people who will work on the farm, let these people acquire in that way a knowledge of the country, and after they have done so let them take up farms of their own and they will be successful to a degree they would not be, under other conditions. i" have said that the policy of my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver) is a policy of occupying the farms of the west and a policy of that kind alone. Let me refer to his statement in the debate on the 15th of January last on this same question. Dealing with a letter written by Mr. Scott to the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Coekshutt) the Minister of the Interior said :
He (Mr. Coekshutt) received his answer and it states the policy of the department, which then and before and since has been to secure settlement of the western lands.
And he follows that up on the next page by saying:
I know it is, but it is my hon. friend and not I who is finding fault. He was at that time with the policy of the government so far as the need of immigrants was concerned, but his policy differed from the policy of the government in that- he wanted to empty the overcrowded tenements of Europe into the citv of Brantford and other cities of Ontario, when the policy of the Dominion government, as stated to him in black and white over the signature of an officer of the department, was to settle the Northwest, to cultivate the prairies, to fill up that western [DOT]ountry in order that there might be employment and business for the commercial and financial interests of eastern Canada.
So that the policy of the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver) is a policy of filling up the farm lands of the west and that alone. We must no doubt fill the farms of the west, but if you bring into this country a hardy agricultural class who will assist our farmers before taking up lands of their own, who will graduate from farms tilled by men who understand the conditions of the country, you will develop this country in the most effective way and you will ensure that those who take up lands will not afterwards abandon them into the hands of speculators and grafters. This government have made no attempt of that kind to assist our farmers, particularly those of the older provinces and enable them to obtain the necessary help from the old country. Will the policy of the minister bring about an improvement in that respect ? I venture to say that when we pay a bonus to a booking agent, his chief effort will be to secure quantity rather than quality and thus increase his commission, and the same may be said of the transportation companies. All these are concerned in procuring the greatest possible number, regardless of quality, and in this way making the greater profit. Their interests are in that sense antagonistic to those of the people of Canada, and while that system continues we shall never acquire that class of immigrants which will be a benefit to our own

farmers. What is the remedy ? I am not called upon to devise a remedy, although it will be but a little time before we on this side will have to propound a remedy. When that time comes I shall be prepared to give my advice in the interests of Canada, but in the meantime it seems to me that we ought to adopt the methods which any business man would use in securing assistance in his business. We might very well establish an Immigration Bureau which would keep a record of the labour required. Our farmers, manufacturers, merchants, miners, railway companies and other interests could then readily communicate with the government through this immigration bureau and inform them of their wants. They could define, not only the number of assistants, they required but also the terms of employment. A farmer for instance would state how many months he would undertake to employ one or more farm hands. When all that information is obtained, then work, not from this end, but from the other end. Employ reliable agents in Britain to come in direct communication with the class of men required and let these agents guarantee that the men they send out are the kind we want. Knowing how many farm labourers are wanted, they will try to obtain them. The responsible agents of the government will take pains to ascertain that the proposed immigrants are actually and bona fide farm hands or as the case may be. They will make arrangements with these people, having 'n mind the condition that exists on this side of the ocean and the actual farmers who want these men. Then they will enter into arrangement for these men to come here, and the farmers here will be advised that the men have come and will be asked to meet the men, make their contracts, and take the men to their homes. If you do this, you will be bringing in a class that will add permanently to the welfare of our country and will assist in supplying our producers with the men thev require.
Now, the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver) seems to think that 160 acres of free land is not a sufficient inducement to the people of Europe and elsewhere to come in and occupy our territory. The hon. minister objected to comparing the conditions of Canada to-day, with its six millions of population! with the conditions of the United States with 80000,000. He said :	I ask you to go back
one hundred and twenty-five years in the history of the United States. But let him take us back any number of years he likes he will not find the United States ever made an offer such as we are making, or gave a bonus such as we are living to bring immigrants into their country. And I ven-tenure to say that neither the United States nor any other country has offered the same Mr. LENNOX.
inducements to hardy, sturdy, self-reliant immigrant that the Dominion of Canada is offering to-day in the lands of the west. We do not need to give prize-packages in order to get rid of these lands. Our west is the greatest and last west available for the teeming millions of Europe. And if you adopt the policy of endeavouring to restrict immigration to the end that none but the fittest should come in, that none but those who measure up to the level of our own citizenship should be allowed to enter, you will have these lands occupied as readily as by depreciating their value and crying them down-which you are doing at the present time by saying in effect: Here is a prize, an inducement for you to come in and settle these lands.
Now, what kind of immigrants are we getting by our efforts? I wish to refer you to some records upon that matter. I do not think that the hardiest and most reckless of the supporters of the government will dare to say that the class of immigrant that we are getting into this country make a better average than those they are getting into the United States. I do not think there is any of these hou. gentlemen quite hardy enough or indifferent enough to the facts to assert that, taken as a class, our immigrants compare favourably with those that go into the United States. Therefore, for a moment, I will direct attention to the class of Immigrants that are going into the United States, even with ail the precautions taken in that country, with all their rigid examinations and in spite of the tax of $4 per head that the immigrants must pay before they can enter that country. Before I go into that, let me say that the hon. member for Lennox (Mr. Uriah Wilson)- a county with a very good name-wrote to tile United States to ascertain whether that country ever paid a bonus to encourage immigration in the reckless and dangerous fashion in which we are endeavouring to encourage it. And he received the following letter from the acting Commissioner of Immigration for the United States :
I have the honour to acknowledge receipt of your letter of the 8th instant, which has been referred to the bureau for attention. So far as I am informed, the United States never solicited immigrants, although no restrictive measures were enacted until 1875, prior to which time foreigners came to the United States of their pleasure.
So they have had restrictions upon immigration ever since 1875. Beginning with a charge of $2 per head, they now charge 84 per head for admitting immigrants to the United States, besides subjecting all to a most rigid examination as to their fitness, physically and otherwise. Let me read a few quotations from the report of Thomas Darlington, M.D., president of the board of health of New York. Under the heading of ' Inspection of School Children in New York City ' he said :

They are subject to a rigid physical examination. During the first three months of 1906, 23,733 children were examined and 17,462 were found to be suffering from some physical abnormality. Of this number of defectives, 12,170, or 70 1 per cent were of foreign birth. It is safe to assume that a large proportion of the remainder were of foreign parentage, for their names give satisfactory evidence of foreign extraction.
In 1905 the 88 children in one truant school in Manhattan were examined. Of these 77 were found to be physically defective; 74 or 96-1 per cent of these latter being of foreign birth. In 1900 about 40 per cent of the school children in the city of New York were foreign born.
In another paragraph of this report I find the following :
An investigation of 500 consecutive deaths of infants from diarrhceal diseases in New York city, shows that 120 or 125 per cent were of native parentage, while 325, or 75 per cent were of foreign parentage. These conditions exist although 63-5 per cent of the total population of New York are natives of the city.
And again :
Practically 33 per cent of the insane-
And this is a very important question.
-in the United States are of foreign birth.
The New York State Lunacy Commission in 1904 reports that 60 per cent of the insane patients in New York city were foreign born. Prom 1885 to 1894 the total admissions to the hospitals for adults of New York city were 282,928; of these 63-7 per cent were of foreign birth. During 1905 there were admitted to 7 of the largest hospitals of the city 26,839 patients ; of these 12,550 or 46 -6 per cent were native born, and 14,289 or 53 4 per cent were foreign born.
So we get a pretty clear idea from this report of the condition of things in the United States. IVith all the rigid examination, with all the care, with all the regulations adopted by the United States, we find that the large percentage of those who are physically unfit are people of foreign birth. Now take our own country. I will read only brief extracts from the inspector of hospitals in Ontario:
There is marked evidence that public attention should be called to the large number of undesirable and unsuitable immigrants that are being induced to seek a shelter in Ontario. This has been found nowhere more noticeable than in the city of Toronto, whore more than half of the indigent casuals, who have had to be provided for, belong to the immigrant class. . . .
The present policy of Canadian emigration agents in Europe would seem to be to secure the number and pay no heed to the quality of persons urged to seek a haven in this country. The system of the Dominion government of bonusing agents to send out in an apparently indiscriminate manner a class of people totally unfit to provide a livelihood for themselves is deplorable.
Further on, and summing up, he says :
But you must have noticed how crime is on the increase in Canada-crime of an abominable character. Evil deeds are rife in this land which we never knew before. Our nation was a better one before these people came.
I do not think there can be any doubt as to that. Now, Mr. Hanna the other day spoke in regard to lunatic asylums, perhaps the most serious phase of the whole question:
We seem to be bringing into this country a cla,ss of people who are going a long way towards peopling (our insane asylums, towards peopling our jails, and towards supplying a pauper population for the cities during the winter time.
Mr. Hanna points out that five years ago, of the total commitments to the insane asylums in Ontario, 20 per cent were foreigners and 80 per cent were Canadians. Now, the percentage of foreigners has increased to 30 per cent, and the percentage of Canadians is 70 per cent. During these five years Mr. Hanna points out that the cost of maintaining those immigrants in Ontario has increased from $24,613.20 to $51,744.30. He shows that last year the total number of patients was 1,162, and of these 346 were immigrants. He also makes a computation, which I presume is correct, to the effect that taking the probable average length of life of these people, the province of Ontario will pay for their maintenance during their lives the sum of $1,487,038.80. He says that of the total population of the province over 16 years of age, 20 per cent are immigrants, or 291,675, and 80 per cent are Canadians, or 1,209,308; but that although the immigrants are ouly 20 per cent of the population, the jail population is composed of 38 per cent of immigrants. and the cost of maintaining them last year was $21,724.65.
Now we have had a large influx of these undesirable people, but for some reason, I think without reason, the Minister of the Interior has seen fit still further to stimulate the bringing in of these people. He cancelled the contract with the North Atlantic Trading Company on the 30th of November, 1906, and we paid no bonuses down to the 19th of February, 1907. From this latter date to the 8th of January last we were giving 5 shillings per head for children, 10 shillings for adults of certain classes, such as farmers, farm labourers, navvies and miners, and 10 shillings for domestic servants. Rut at a time when every city in this Dominion was groaning under the weight of taxation, voluntary taxation it is true, brought about by the invasion of these helpless people, this government, with a recklessness which has nwt been explained, saw fit to double the bonus to be paid, and no earthly reason can be suggested for it unless it be some ulterior motive of assisting those pets of the government who are in

some mysterious way brought into relations with the government in order to bring about this immigration.
Could any sane government imagine for a moment, that, at a time when every city in this country was complaining of the presence of foreigners who were a tax upon the generosity of the good people of those cities, when every jail was more than crowded by the class of people who had been brought to this country, it was necessary or wise for the Minister of the Interior to double the bonus and thereby increase the difficulty under which this country was groaning ? What was the bonus for ? I have only heard one explanation-that it was for the purpose of enabling the booking agents to advertise Canada in foreign lands. I would like to ask the Minister of the Interior-and before he joined the government he was a sensible man-who should do this advertising? Do we always want middlemen intervening in the affairs of Canada or, if we have to advertise Canada, would it not be better that the people of Canada should do their own advertising and not- go to middlemen such as the North Atlantic Trading Company was and such as these men now are not knowing even whether the money has been expended or not ? If I remember rightly, if there has been anything that the minister has boasted about or prided himself upon it has been, in this House and on the public platform, to let the labour party know that he was not hand in glove with the Manufacturers' Association, that, in fact, he was hostile to the Manufacturers' Association. Is the government honest with labour unions and skilled labour? I want to know and tomorrow the labour unions, and skilled labour. will want to know, whether the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Smith) has been honest to-day or not, and I think they will bring in a verdict adverse to that hon. gentleman. I want to say definitely and emphatically that all the evidence goes to show that the government have been playing a double game in this matter, that they have not been honest with the labour unions or skilled labour but they have been playing into the hands of the Manufacturers Association, while they [DOT]pretended by their speeches to the labour party that they were fighting the Manufacturers' Association. The Minister of the Interior, like his brave supporter to-night, made a vicious attack upon the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) and I think in that regard he did not go too far, if he was judicious, because he had a foeman worthy of his steel. He realized that the hon. member for Brantford was doing the government very serious harm in regard to their , immigration policy, but in the discussion he brought in some questions which resulted in the hon. member for Brantford retaliating. Among other things the hon. member read a letter which came from where?-which Mr. LENNOX.
came from the Department of the Interior- and which showed pretty conclusively the attitude of the government in regard to skilled labour in this country. Now, I will read that letter and I will point out to you, Mr. Speaker, in connection with the reading of it, that the Minister of the Interior did not dare to ask that the hon. member from Brantford should give the name of the official, who sent out this letter. Why? Because if he had got the name be would have been bound, if this gentleman had done wrong to call him to account. The only reason I can suggest in connection with the matter is that he knew perfectly well from the tone of the letter that it 'was in accordance with the express or implied instructions of the government to that official and he dared not call him to account. Here is what the letter says. It is an unsolicited letter which shows what the minister calls the aggressive immigration movement of the government :
Interior Department of the government of Canada.
Immigration branch,
Agent, ,Tohn McLennan,
26 Guild Stret,
Aberdeen, June 3, 1907. W. F. Cockshutt, Esq.,
Brantford, Out., Can.
Dear Sir,-I see by reports of various newspapers, that numerous members of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association are in need of skilled and unskilled help. As representatives of the government here, we have many inquiries from skilled mechanics in nearly all branches of the trade, desiring information about opportunities for their line in Canada and having no specific information we must be governed in our replies by general terms and conditions.
That looks like a desire on the part of the government to be put in a position of supplying necessary information to these men who are making inquiries in order that they might come and find homes and employment in the labour market of Canada and to that extent, come into rivalry with the skilled and union labour men of Canada. This letter goes on :
I believe that if the secretary of your association would supply the government offices from time to time, of which the inclosed is a list; of the needs of your association, that it will be of great practical assistance in securing some of the needed help, say for instance, in this form, that there are so many carriage blacksmiths, so many boilermakers, lathe men, moulders, carriage builders and so forth wanted If we had such a list as that in our hands we could give definite assurance to men that they could get work, and then refer them to the headquarters of your association in Toronto, Montreal or other large centres, for distribution.
That looks like wanting to enter ipto a contract with the Manufacturers' Associa-

tion, to concur with them and carry on this aggressive propaganda, which the Minister of the Interior is so fond of speaking of-in bringing into Canada skilled labour in competition with the skilled labour of Canada. It goes on :
I make this as a suggestion, as we are quite often at a loss what to say, not having any definite information respecting the needs of numerous lines of work, for which we have inquiries here.
I am directing this communication to you, as I believe that you are the president of the association or was, the last information that I had.
Mark you what he wants done.
I know in any event that you will forward it to the proper authorities, in the event that you are not at present the active executive of the association I will be glad in any event to hear from you, your opinion respecting this suggestion.
Very truly yours,
john Mclennan,
Canadian government agent.
And the Minister of the Interior recognizing the significance of one of the his principal agents in the old country coming into direct conflict with the organized labour unions and skilled mechanics of this country, did not dare to ask the hon. member (Mr. Coekshutt) the name of his informant. Do the union men of this country want more conclusive or damning evidence of the guilt of the government and of the minister than the production of that letter? I do not think so. But the Minister of the Interior even though he be not always brave is daring, and he concluded his eloquent but irrelevant speech by reading a document which was issued by a certain historical personage whose alias is Lazarus. Was it not daring and indiscret for the minister to mention Lazarus or Leopold in 9 connection with immigration. He read a letter to show that Mr. Leopold was advertising as follows :
This week's vacancies are: fitters, turners, joiners, labourers, tinsmiths, toolmakers, coat-makers, brushmakers, hammersmiths, chair-makers, cottonweavers, brass workers, cabinetmakers. Daper mill engineers, wood working machinists. Fresh vacancies from Canada by each mail. Girls! Girls! Girls! Also families, high wages, assisted passages. Experienced and inexperienced machinists for straw hats, caps, whitewear, tailoring. Mill hands for knitting, woollen and cotton mills. Chocolate dippers, &c., &c.
And the Minister of the Interior said this was signed by Mr. Louis Leopold on behalf of the Manufacturers' Association. Who brought Leopold from oblivion into the position he occupies ? Who but this present government, and who but the Minister of the Interior and his predecessor. Have the people of Canada forgotten that this Louis Leopold alias Lazarus who was picking up large crumbs at the expense of
the people of Canada was the man who acted hand in hand with W. T. R. Preston, who is still in the employ of the government, and as to whose acts although the government promised an investigation they dare not investigate. It was this Mr. Lazarus who had an office in the same building with Mr. Preston when he was representing the government in England, it is this man whom the Minister of the Interior resorts to in an endeavour to refute certain facts. The chickens have come home to roost. Such an incident opens the eyes of the labour unions and the skilled mechanics of this country who are struggling to make an honest and competent living, and who have been befooled far too long by this government. Now, I want to revert to a statement made by the Minister of the Interior in this debate on April 13, when he thought fit to refer to the amendment to the immigration law passed this session, and to the attitude of the opposition in connection with it. He said :
It is not long since in an effort to make it possible to carry out our understanding and to complete the fulfilment of our obligations, there was before the House a little amendment to the Immigration Act, a trifling little matter of some four or five lines.
Mark you, this was to enable the government, as he said, to carry out their understanding with one nation, evidently meaning Japan.
We had to face an immigration question on the Pacific coast as well as on the Atlantic, and it is different on the Pacific from what it is on the Atlantic.
I agree in that.
The immigration differs at every point of the compass. It is necessary to adopt a restrictive policy on the Pacific coast.
You will see what restrictive policy they have adopted because I intend to charge that here again the government have not been guilty of honesty. I do not want to use any harsher term, but I say that the government have not been guilty of being candid either with the people of British Columbia or with the labour party of this country.
Different measures were suggested with regard to that restrictive policy, but it was thought well in the interests of the country, in the interests of the empire, that a conciliatory rather than an aggressive policy should be adopted in connection with one country at any rate.
Evidently meaning Japan.
In pursuance of that idea an amicable arrangement was arrived at with that country, and it is hoped that a similar arrangement can be arrived at with another that is in a somewhat similar position in regard to immigration. But an agreement with Japan as to the restrictions on immigrants from Japan to Can-

ada or an agreement with the government of India as to the restriction of immigrants from India to Canada was of no value without the provision we asked this House to pass the other night. It was absolutely of no effect.
Mark you, they could not work out their policy with Japan or with India unless they got this legislation. I want to say, not only has the government added additional shackles to Canada in the matter of immigration by the Act they passed the other day, but at the present moment Canada, by reason of the treaty, by reason of negotiations of the Minister of Labour, and by reason of the final crystallization into law of that whole matter, stands in the most humiliating and degrading and despicable position of any nominally free nation in the world.
I want to say to the people of British Columbia, I want to say to the labour people of Canada and to all the people of Canada, that we are tied hand and foot as regard^ the question of immigration, by reason of the treaty with Japan, the treaty being, as the right hon. gentleman said the other day, above the law with regard to immigration wnich we put on our statute-book. My right hon. friend shakes his head. I do not go by a shake of the head ; I go by the records of this House, and I refer to what was said the other day when we were debating this matter, and when the right hon. gentleman said that as between the statute we were passing and the treaty, the treaty should prevail over the statute; and so it does as a matter of fact, whether the right hon. gentleman had said it or not. Now, what have we done? As the Minister of the Interior said, we had to pass this law. There were negotiations, and we had to satisfy Japan. The right hon. gentleman said: Japan is a sensitive nation; it is willing to be treated on the same basis as other nations, but is not willing to be discriminated against. The right hon. gentleman has made it clear that we are in this position, that whatever restrictive laws Japan may have as regards emigration from its shores, Canada is not allowed by Japan to enact any legislation which will conflict with Japan uuless Canada enacts similar legislation with regard to every other country in the world, including Great Britain itself. A sensitive nation, the right hon. gentleman says. Yes; yet in 1905, when the treaty between Great Britain and Japan was in force, Australia demanded free action as regards immigration, and Australia got that concession from Japan. A sensitive nation! Yes, sensitive when Canada has only a population of six millions, but not sensitive towards the United States when the United States lias a population of eighty millions: and in 1904. the same year in which the treaty with Great Britain was consummated. Japan conceded to the United States the right which we should have safeguarded in our treaty with Japan. Sensi-

tive? Is no one to be sensitive in Canada? Are we to have no national pride? Are we to surrender the right of making our own laws, and submit to the indignity of having our laws in regard to immigration made at Tokio, as in fact they are at the present time? Just follow out this legislation. Before the other day we had this provision:
The Governor in Council may, by proclamation or order, whenever he considers it necessary or expedient, prohibit the landing in Canada of any specified class of immigrants, of which due notice shall be given to the transportation conpanies.
The hon. Minister of the Interior says that means a certain class as regards occupation, not as regards a country, and I think he is right as to that. Then the government the other day introduced an Act wnich was intended to get over difficulties

which was intended to prevent Japanese coming to Canada, which was intended to keep the Hindus out of British Columbia. and it was proclaimed to the people of British Columbia as having that effect. It has not that effect, and the right hon. gentleman and the Minister of the Interior well know it. Here is the form in which the Act was introduced:
The Governor in Council may, by proclamation or order, whenever he considers it necessary or expedient, prohibit the landing in Canada of any specified class of immigrants-
That was in the old Act, and in the new we read:
-or of any immigrants who, being natives or citizens of any specified country, have come to Canada otherwise than by continuous journey from that country on through tickets purchased there.
That was the Act as it was introduced. But when it came to be considered by this House, that would not do. That gave us too much liberty. That enabled us to specify Japan; it enabled us to say that if the labour market was congested, the Governor in Council could make an order that Japanese artisans or mechanics or labourers should not come in. But we dare not do that, because the right hon. leader of this House says that Japan is a sensitive nation, and is only willing that we should legislate in the same way in regard to Japan that we do in regard to other countries. And so what we must do in order not to offend Japan is to surrender our rights. We have, as he told the hon. member for South Lanark (Mr. Haggart), the right to shut out British subjects if we like; we can shut them out with reason or without reason. But, the right hon. gentleman says by his action and the action of his ministers, we cannot do that with regard to Japan. The Minister of the Interior says this parliament is supreme, but in the same breath he asks us to mutilate the statute which he brought in, and it was passed in this form:

-or any immigrants wlio have come to Canada otherwise than by continuous journey from the country of which they are natives or citizens and upon through tickets purchased in such country.
What is the meaning of that ? The difference is this: that we had the right to specify any country under the Act as it was introduced. But Japan would not stand that; we dare not do it. And now by the change made the only order in council that can be passed is an order which excludes everybody-which puts Australia and every other British possession, which puts Great Britain itself, on the same line of exclusion that we adopt in reference to Japan. That is the position we are in. We are bouusing immigrants; it is the boast of this government that we are endeavouring to get British immigration into this country. British immigrants come to Canada, remain for a year, and then go to the United States. British immigrants go to the United States, remain there a year or two, and want to come to Canada. An order in council has to be passed. That order in council confronts them at the border, and it is said to them; You are British subjects; you have never foresworn your allegiance to the British Crown; you are of us, but you cannot come in. That is what the law does. We are endeavouring to get immigrants from Holland; the Hollander must come by direct course or he cannot come at all. We are endeavouring to get the citizens of France; they must come direct from France or they cannot come at all- -why? Because Japan says so. Take every country from which we are seeking immigration, and we are confronted with the mandate of Japan. It is by the mandate of Japan that we have had to pass this law, which will exclude British subjects unless they come direct, which will exclude the people of the best nations of Europe unless they come direct, which will exclude the citizens of the United States unless they came direct, which will exclude everybody unless he comes direct, or else we have to leave that law a dead letter. Is the hon. gentleman going to enforce that law? No. He says to the labour people of British Columbia: I have passed a law which will be your protection. I say to the Minister of the Interior that no more humiliating condition ever existed in Canada or in any other country than that which exists by reasou of the attitude of this government in regard to that treaty with Japan. Although I desire that we should have friendly relations with that nation, yet rather than feel that we in this free country have surrendered our rights as a sovereign people to make our own laws with regard to immigration and have consented to have our laws made at Tokio, I for one would be prepared at any moment to denounce the treaty we have with Japan at the present time.

The resolution which my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk! has presented is one of vast importance to every portion of the Dominion. It is of special importance to the western country, and that must be my excuse for my taking up a short time of the House to-night. The hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Lennox) passed a few compliments to the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Smith). He said that the hon. member for Nanaimo was now opposed to the labour party. Well, 1 would venture the statement that the labour party in Canada have not in the whole Dominion a better or a truer friend than my hon. friend from Nanaimo. He has given evidence of his devotion to the labour party time and again and be has, as a big broad-minded man, done more for the labour interests in Canada than any otliet man in public life. The hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) argued that because my hon. friend from Nanaimo supported this government he was therefore opposed to the labour party. But that does not follow by any means. No one who is not a blind partisan will deny that no government in Canada has ever done so much for the labour interests as the present administration. I would venture the statement that the labour party themselves acknowledge this. I do not say that every individual does, but the labour interests as a whole are convinced that this government has done more for them than any previous administration.
Then we had the hon. gentleman arguing that the government are discriminating in their immigration policy against the province of Quebec and the other eastern provinces. Well, would he advocate that this government should spend money to take thousands of people from Quebec or Ontario up to Manitoba or Saskatchewan or Alberta or British Columbia? I venture to say that any hon. gentleman who would move a resolution to that effect would be laughed out of court. It is not the duty of this or any government to remove population from one part of the Dominion to the other. Is not a good citizen in Quebec or Ontario wortlj as much to the Dominion, earning his living there, industrious and contented, as he would be if we were to remove him to the west ? As representing a western constituency, I should certainly not be inclined to support any such proposition any more than I would be disposed to support a proposal that the government should pay out money for the purpose of taking settlers from Saskatchewan or Alberta and bringing them down here. The policy is so absurd that one wonders how any reasonable man could think of suggesting it.
The hon. gentleman also claims that the policy of this government on immigration is not in favour of the farming community. That statement rather surprised me, be-

cause if there is any part of the community which benefits by that policy it is our farming population. What are the classes of people on whom this government pays a bonus for bringing them out? They are first of all the farmers and farm labourers, then female domestic servants and under certain circumstances railway navvies. Those are the only classes on whom we are paying a bonus, and even with the payment of this bonus we have not been able, although we have been giving special consideration to the agricultural class, to secure sufficient labour. My hon. friend suggests that it is not farmers, but farm labourers to which the government should specially devote its attention. Would any sensible man prefer, as a settler, a farm labourer to a farmer who would own and work his own farm ? I do not think that the class of farm labourers, those who would be content to always remain farm labourers, is the most desirable class and the one we most require. What we specially want are men who will, if you like, work as labourers for a year or two and then take up farms of their own, or who will, if they have the means, take up a farm at once. I think, therefore, that the government is doing what is the very best in the interest of the farming community.
The hon. gentleman tried to create the impression that the west is receiving the greatest benefit from the policy of this government. Let me tell him that the province from which he comes is that which gets by far the largest number of immigrants. Ontario gets far more immigrants than Manitoba or Saskatchewan or Alberta or British Columbia or any other province. 1 have here a statement of the number of immigrants who have gone into each province every year. Take the last three years for instance. Ontario got in 1906 52,000 ; in 1907, 32,000, and in 1908, 70,000.
The hon. gentleman must be wrong because we are only beginning 1908.

I mean the nine months of the fiscal year 1907-8. Quebec received
25.000	in 1906, 18,000 in 1907 and 40,000 in the nine months of 1907-8. Manitoba received 35,000 in 1906, 20,000 in 1907 and
36.000	in the nine months of 1907-8. Taking the totals from 1901 to the present time we find the immigrants were divided as follows :
Ontario	 243,117
Quebec	 164,371
Manitoba	 230,946
Saskatchewan and Alberta	 299,949
So, it will be seen that if this is a western policy it is also a Dominion policy, it builds up the east as well as the west, the immigrants being sent largely where they want to go. Of course, you cannot make people go to the maritime provinces if they wish to go to the prairies; you cannot make Mr. TURRIFF.
them go to Ontario if they prefer to go to Quebec. But the government gives information and what guidance it may and does not interfere with their going to one province or the other. The immigrants have distributed themselves and the province of Ontario, from which the hon. gentleman comes, has received far more immigrants than any other province of the Dominion.
The hon. member also stated that it would be but a short time before they would be on this side of the House, and they would find a remedy. I can only say to the hon. member again that he and his friends were on this side for eighteen long years. And, by the way, the hon. gentleman spoke this afternoon about prize-packages, saying they were not necessary in order to secure the occupation of our western lands. But, if is is so easy to settle up these lands now why did not his friends do something during the eighteen years they were on this side of the House ? They had time enough to experiment; but what they succeeded in doing was not in bringing a million immigrants into Canada but in sending a million emigrants from Canada into the United States. That is the difference between the policy of the government under its successive Ministers of the Interior and that pursued by hon. gentlemen opposite. I doubt that the people of Canada, knowing what was done by hon. gentlemen opposite during their eighteen years of office to populate that western country as well as the rest of Canada, will give these hon. gentlemen the mandate to find a remedy for this policy, for there is no remedy needed. Things are going very well; the country is prospering-
For a portion of the people.

Yes, it is going very well for nine hundred and ninety-nine out of a thousand of the people. You can go to any part of the Dominion and you will not find very much grumbling. The hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) said that if the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver) had stated that there were ten men out of employment now for one out of employment ten years ago, he would have been nearer the truth. I do not think the hon. member (Mr. Cockshutt) will find many to back him up in that statement. I remember very well, as I am sure most of us do, the condition of things ten years ago, and I doubt if any hon. gentleman except the member for Brantford will say that the conditions for employment of labour were as good then as they are now. And I venture to say that at this moment-and the same would be true of any time during the past six months-notwithstanding the talk about unemployed people in Toronto, Montreal, Winnipeg and others of our larger cities, there has not been employment for every man in the Dominion who was will-

iug to go to where the work was and to do the work when he got there. What is the reason that people are unemployed? Simply because they would not do the work offered them. Some, perhaps, were not suited to the work. A gentleman from Winnipeg who came down to-day told me that he had the greatest difficulty during the past few months in securing farm labourers. He offered $25 a month and board and could not get men to work. He hired a number who promised to go but afterwards would not go. Certain people will not live in the country; they congregate in the cities and complain if they do not get work there. 1 believe the statement cannot be refuted that at no time during the past five years has there been more labour In Canada than the demand for labour, except in a few places where there has been overcrowding because the people were not willing to go where they could get work. The hon, member also made the statement that the United States were getting a much better class of immigrants than Canada is getting. How any man can make a statement like that is more than I can undei'stand. As stated several times in this debate, the United States do not pay a bonus on immigrants, nor have they any immigration agents authorized to carry on work in European countries. Further than that, they put a head tax on immigrants for the purpose of keeping the people out. X believe that the mover of this resolution, the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) and almost every hon. member on that side who has spoken in this debate has advocated the adoption by Canada of the same measures as have been adopted in the United States. Well, if the result of adopting those measures should be the same as what we see in the United States, God forbid that we should adopt them. For, as has been pointed out by the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Ralph Smith) 65 per cent of the immigration going into the United States- and it is going in now at the rate of a million and a quarter people a year-comes from a portion of Europe that we look upon as undesirable, the southern countries, in which oountries we do not carry on an immigration propaganda or from which we do not seek to induce immigrants to come to this country. On the other hand, not more than ten per cent of our immigrants come from these countries. In fact, if you exclude the Japanese and the Hindus you find that only six or seven per cent of the total immigration into Canada comes from such countries as southern Italy and other places in the south of Europe and in Asia that we do not look upon as desirable fields of immigration. I say we do not vfant. to adopt the same methods as are adopted by the United States, if they are going to bring about the same results. I have no doubt that if we did adopt those mjethods the result would be exactly the same.
A good deal of objection has been taken during this debate by members on the other side of the House to the system of paying bonuses, and they claim that all the undesirables that come into Canada are brought in. practically, by the bonus system. Now I do not pretend that there are no undesirables coming into Canada. You cannot bring in a quarter of a million people per annum without having some of the lower classes among them. But the very fact that we pay a bonus enables us to select our people. The bonus, as has been pointed out, is not paid to the settler, and it is not paid to the booking agent primarily for the purpose of inducing him to secure immigrants for Canada. The object of the bonus that is paid to the booking agent is this : The booking agent gets a commission on the tickets that he sells. If he sells an expensive ticket his percentage is naturally a great deal more than if he sells a cheap ticket. A steerage passage ticket from Europe to Canada will cost about $25 or $27. The commission on that ticket does not amount to nearly as much as the commission on a ticket to the Argentine Republic, to Australia or New Zealand, or Brazil, or many of the other countries which are anxious to get immigrants. Naturally therefore the desire of the booking agent is to sell the ticket to wherever he can make the most money on it. So in order to offset the inducement they would have of advocating these other countries and directing settlers to go there, the government steps in and gives them a bonus on all the people of a certain class that the booking agent can direct to Canada. Now what is the result ? Suppose that five men of different occupations go to a booking agent in order to get information. They want to find out about Canada, about Australia, about New Zealand and about the Argentine Republic. If there is a farmer amongst them or a farm labourer, the booking agent naturally, for his own benefit, advises that farmer or that farm labourer to buy a ticket to Canada, because, although he gets a smaller percentage from the steamship company, he gets a bonus from Canada. But if among the five men there are three who do not belong to the classes on which we pay a bonus, the agent does not advise them to come to Canada. Why ? Because he gets no bonus on them, and if he sells them a ticket he makes a smaller commission. But if he can persuade that man to go to the Argentine Republic, or to New Zealand, or to Australia, he sells a much higher priced ticket and he gets a larger commission. So the result is that the payment of this bonus has exactly the opposite effect that speakers on the other side of the House have tried to make out all through this debate. It has the effect of bringing the right class of people to Canada, and it has the effect of keeping the

class of people that we do not want out of Canada, and directing them to the other countries who do want them. Those are the facts of the case, and they cannot be controverted.
The hon. member was very anxious to know why the government had doubled the bonus. I will tell him why. It is because we want more settlers. We want more settlers in the western country. I do not know whether the people of Ontario and Quebec want more settlers to settle up their farm lands, because those provinces have millions of acres of good land yet to settle. Wheu the government of Ontario a few years ago sent out men to inspect the north land, they found one stretch of 1(3,000,000 acres of good land. You have to think for a moment in order to realize what 10,000,000 acres of land means. It means as much laud, I think, as is cultivated in the jirovince of Ontario at the present time ; at all events, it means about three times as much land as we have cultivated in the three western provinces on which we have raised in some years as much as 200,000,000 bushels of grain, besides all the cattle. There is any amount of land in Ontario being opened up at the present time by the Temiscaming and Northern Railway, and by the new Grand Trunk Pacific. The same remarks apply to the province of Quebec. In the hinterland of Quebec there are many millions of acres of good land. Does not the Dominion of Canada want to have these lands settled up ? Does not Ontario want to have her lands settled up ? Does not Quebec want to have her lauds settled up ? I do not think any one will say for a moment that these lands should not be settled up as quickly as possible. The bonus has been doubled iD order to bring out more settlers, and because we are getting settlers of the right class. I know that in the western provinces, for which I can speak, we are getting the most satisfactory class of people.
Now almost every speaker on the other side of the House has reflected on the character of the immigrants that come from the continent of Europe. I want to say, Mr. Speaker, that I have seen hundreds and thousands of those settlers in the northwestern provinces : I have driven through their settlements, I have stopped at their farms, I have entered their houses, and I want to say that you cannot go to any country in the world and find better settlers than the Icelanders, than the Germans, than the Swedes, than the Norwegians, than the Hungarians, than even the Galicians, who have been ridiculed so much by hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House.
I want to say that the Galicians are a good class of people, they make good settlers for the western country. We have thousands of Galicians who have settled on lands that the ordinary English speaking Mr. TURRIFF.
settler from the old country, or from Canada or the United States, would not have settled on at all, for the present at all events, land that they would not take as a gift. But these Galicians have gone on those lands and have made good farms out of them and are becoming prosperous. I venture the assertion that within twenty-five years from this date the Galicians in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, will, as a class, be the wealthiest farmers in that country. Besides being able to make themselves comfortable, they are good settlers, because the first thing a Galician learns is to say, [DOT] Me Canadian.' He wants to become a Canadian at once. He wants to forget his Austrian way of living, he wants to forget his Austrian way of farming. Wheu you And a Galician settlement and an English speaking farmer in the near vicinity, you will find them going out three or four at a time and spending hours watching him doing his work. Inside of two or three years, drive up to a Galician house, or to his farmyard, and until you speak to him and And that he speaks broken English, you would not think, by looking at bis place, that he was not a settler from the province of Ontario. If you wanted to teach them the Galician language in the schools they would not accept it. They say, no, I want my children to learn English, I want my child to be a Canadian; we can teach them the Galician language at home, but we want them to learn English in the schools. They have the right spirit all through, and are a clever people. They have been criticised simply because when they first came out after a months' travel on land and water, they are not as finely dressed as our settlers would be going up from this country. They have their Austrian style of wool or sheepskin coats which look a little incongruous perhaps, but, in a year or two, you do not know these people. They are just as fine a class of settlers as we have in Canada. I have none in my constituency, so I am not saying this for the sake of catching any Galician votes.
We thought you were.
Yes, but you are very often mistaken wheu you have thoughts like that; you are entitled to another think.
You are helping your friends.

While hon. members may decry the policy of the government for party purposes, their friends in the west will not deny it, because it is filling up the west, it is building up the west; and not only is it building up the west but it is building up the whole Dominion of Canada; because you cannot build up one part of the country and make it prosperous without helping all parts of the country.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I apologize for having taken up so much of the time of the House. But I regard this as a subject of special importance to Canada, and of special importance to the west, and I felt justified in trying to offset in some degree the very erronous impression sought to be made by hon. members on the other side of the House throughout this discussion.

Then he has spoken of the wonderful results of the efforts of this government in regard to immigration. The hon. member for Strathcona (Mr. McIntyre) was good enough to devote some of his attention to myself and he did not seem inclined to accept the statement which I had made when in the west as to the speech which I had delivered at Valleyfield, I think it was. The hon. gentleman showed himself to be the champion of the North Atlantic Trading Company. He portrayed to this House the advantages which resulted from the North Atlantic Trading Company. There is one thing that he forgot; he forgot to explain how it was that so valuable and beneficient a contract as that which existed between this government and the North Atlantic Trading Company was put an end to by the government. * Why did not my hon. friend rise in his place in parliament when the hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver) announced the termination of the contract and protest against it if it were so valuable a contract as he has endeavoured to make it appear. If the hon. gentleman desires any statement with regard to the character of the Galician immigrants he had better not refer so much to my remarks as to those of the hon. Minister of the Interior. In 1901 I listened in this House to the remarks of the hon. Minister of the Interior with regard to these immigrants. Does my hon. friend from Strathcona concur in that gentleman's statement as to their character ? He has read it ; will he state now whether he
approves of it or repudiates it ? My hon. friend seems to regard that as a conundrum which he is unable to answer. I listened to the diatribes of the Minister of the Interior. I was influenced to some extent by them. I went west next year myself, I came back from the west and in the year 1903 and again in 1904 I said to this House that I had been subject to some prejudice against these people principally on account of the remarks of the hon. Minister of the Interior, but that I had gone to the west and I had been agreeably disappointed, that I believed the Galicians would make good settlers and I repeat the statement now and state my belief that we would hardly be able to distinguish the second generation from the sons and daughters of Canadians in the west. Last year I repeated to my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior his own remarks characterizing these people in the most scandalous terms and what answer did I get from the Minister of the Interior?
