Thus, if the hon. member for Strathcona wishes to learn the opinion of his leader, which he is not willing either to approve or repudiate, let him turn to the debates of 1901 and commit to memory some of the adjectives which were applied by his present leader to the Galicians. So much for that portion of the matter, except that I want to say one or two words about certain remarks of my hon. friend from Nanaimo (Mr. Smith). He has been answered on all points, I think, except one, and that is the one I desire to mention. He declared in this House and he gave me an evasive answer to what I thought was a courteous question that the motion of my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier was designed to do away with all efforts to promote immigration to this country. There are no such words in the resolution. My hon. friend from Nanaimo knew that perfectly well when he made that statement. The motion of the hon. member for Jacques Cartier simply declared that while it is desired to maintain the efforts to promote desirable and legitimate immigration the time to pay bonuses has ceased; that is all.
Let us look for one minute at the merits of the question itself because I desire to be very brief indeed. Before doing so, however, just let me make one remark. We have had speeches from three or four gentlemen from the west, but from not one of them have we had a single reference to the 200,000 lost immigrants who ought to be in the west but who are not there according to the census returns. Does the member for Strathcona know where they are. Have they been destroyed in some great catastrophe ; are they hidden in some remote corner of the Northwest, have they
*

gone to the United States, or did they exist only for the purpose of paying bonuses to the North Atlantic Trading Company. In the old days the Minister of Customs made the welkin ring while discanting on these discrepancies between the immigration returns and the census returns, but now there is not one word from him or from his. friends as to the whereabouts of these 200,000 lost souls who are supposed to be in the west if the immigration returns are to be believed.
The total immigration to this country, according to a government return, from 1896 to 1907-1908 (nine months) was 1,209,437 ; the bonused immigration was 250,259 and the non-bonused immigration 959,179. Less than one-fifth of the total immigration during that period was bonused. During the very last year the total immigration into Canada was 235,235, the bonused immigration 20,516, and the non-bonused immigration 215,000. Can any hon. member of this House tell me how many of these 20,000 bonused immigrants would not have come to Canada if there was no bonus paid. I am not one of those who believe in the glib story often repeated on the other side of the House about men going to booking agents to decide for them the country in which they shall make their future home. I am firmly of opinion that very few of these 20,000 bonused immigrants would have been lost to Canada if we had paid no bonus at all. We got 215,000 people to come to Canada last year on the merits of Canada and by properly advertising Canada, and on 20,000 immigrants only did we pay a bonus. And when we realize that a very great majority of these
20,000	would come to Canada in any case what man of common sense will say that the motion of my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) is not absolutely right, and that the time has come to cease giving a bonus for immigrants.
Let us see how these bonuses have been paid during past years. From 1898 to the present time we have paid in bonuses on British immigratns $252,230.89, on United States immigrants, $82,571.97, but on continental European immigrants we have paid no less than $445,811.16, making a total altogether of $781,613.96. I have already said in the House that bonusing might be justifiable under certain conditions and for the purpose of obtaining settlers of a specially excellent type; but I have never heard it claimed that the 20,000 immigrants that came last year under the bonus were of any better class than those who came without the payment of a bonus.
The hon. member for Perth (Mr. McIntyre) called attention to some remarks I made in the House last year when the hon. member for Montmagny moved a resolution in the exact words which the Minister of Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
the Interior used before he took office. On that occasion I said:
I was impressed with the baldness of this resolution wlien my hon. friend from Montmagny (Mr. Lavergne) moved it. But its somewhat bald and abrupt wording was explained afterwards when it was shown to consist of two sentences taken from two speeches of the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver). It could not therefore be expected to be in precisely that form which would command the adhesion of a majority in this House.
Let us look at it for a few minutes and see what it involves. It declares that the payment of bonuses on immigrants has a tendency to bring a less desirable rather than a more desirable class of people into this country. That was the utterance of my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver) some few years ago before he was a minister of the Crown. I do not think that sentence expresses a principle in which 1 would be inclined to confer. It does not seem to me that the payment of bonuses in itself has any tendency to bring in a less rather than a more desirable class of people into this country. That would depend altogether on the way you work it out. If without the payment of bonuses you permit people to come in indiscriminately, if you use every possible means by advertising and otherwise in any particular country from which immigration is not very desirable, you might, without a system of bonusing at all, increase the tendency to bring in people who are not desirable. On the other hand, if you use the system of bonusing, you might attach to it such conditions as would not tend to bring in undesirable people.
I adhere to that statement to-night. I do not see one word in it that is at all inconsistent with the motion of my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk). The motion of my hon. friend from Montmagny last year with regard to which I spoke was this :
That the payment of bonuses on immigration has a tendency to bring in a less rather than a more desirable class of people, that it is a most unwise policy and expenditure and therefore should not be continued.
If the hon. member for Perth (Mr. McIntyre) were here, I would ask him if he is prepared to extend the same words of commendation to this language of the Minister of the Interior before he took office, as he did to the more recent utterances of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Oliver) in regard to this matter. At all events the words quoted in the motion of my hon. friend (Mr. Lavergne) are entirely inconsistent with those the Minister of the Interior has since uttered.
Reference has been made to the settlers from the United States who are going into the Canadian west. Having seen something of these settlers during the past year, I am prepared to say that I do not believe there is a better class of settlers in the western provinces than those which have come from the United States. I have seen them in

Alberta and Saskatchewan especially. 1 have found them imbued with the spirit of our institutions, understanding the principles of responsible government and immediately upon their arrival in this country prepared to take an interest in our public affairs and to assume the full duties of citizenship. I do not think we have anything to fear from settlers of that kind. My hon. friend from Perth alluded to what he termed the spirit of sentiment of Canadian citizenship) and the impossibility of our obtaining at the present juncture people from all countries in the world who fully comprehend' the spirit of responsible government. I do not doubt at all that men who come from continental European countries which enjoy in some measure at least responsible government will make thoroughly good citizens, but at the same time I believe it to be most desirable so far as possible to bring into Cauada and especially into the great west, only those who are already acquain-ed by active participation, with the duties and the responsibilities and the privileges of that same responsible government which we enjoy in Canada. Let us not forget that criticism has been made upon the English speaking nations of the world-that, the principles of democratic government are only in an experimental stage, and that the day may come when there will be some reversion from the system which we now enjoy, and more absolute system will take its place, for the very reason that men engaged in the haste and pressure of the affairs of every day life are not inclined to give to the service of the state that proportion of their time and energy which is necessary if we are to attain the highest standards of democratic responsible government. If there be anything in that criticism-and perhaps it would not be well to minimize it too greatly-it is certainly desirable that we should get in this country as far s possible men of the type I have described ; and therefore, while for, the most part, I concur in that regard in what my hon. friend from South Perth has said, I still insist that a great deal of care should be taken in the line of what I have just now suggested.
Of the character of the immigration that is coming into this country, I do not propose to speak by way of distinguishing one nationality from another. I propose to speak of it by way of distinguishing those of any particular nation who are fit from those of that same nation who are not fit to become citizens of Canada. We have gathered some rather important information on this point reported to us from the events of the past year and of the past six months, and I propose to refer for a few moments to a very notable speech-which unfortunately has not been very fully reported- delivered by the hon. Provincial Secretary of Ontario not very long ago. The fullest
report of that speech that I have been able to obtain uses the following language :
During 1907 there were 1,163 admitted to asylums of the province, of whom 346 were foreign born.	'
Mr. Hanna was evidently using the expression ' foreign-born ' to indicate those born out of this country.
During the past five years the perecentage of foreigners admitted to these institutions had increased from twenty to thirty per cent, while Canadian born patients had decreased from eighty to seventy per cent. In the same period, from 1903 to 1907, the cost of maintenance of foreign horn patients had increased from $24,613.20 to $51,744.30. While the foreign horn of the entire adult population were only twenty per cent, the total admissions to asylums from that class was thirty per cent. The figures showed the necessity of effective methods to prevent the dumping of undesirables by friends and others aided by charitable associations with no other object than to get rid of the responsibility of providing for them. Taking into consideration the probable length of life of these patients, the cost of maintaining those jadmitted in 1907 alone would amount to $1,487,038.80, without including any proportion for capital expenditure.
That statement attracted my attention to such an extent that I sent to Mr. Hanna and asked him for particulars of it, and I have here the particulars which I will take the liberty of bringing to the attention of the House. The statement on which he bases it is this :
For future maintenance we find that the expectation of life (Carlisle) at age 37 (the average of foreign horn patients) is 29-64 years; and assuming that the cost of maintenance is $145 per patient per annum (which is a low estimate) the total future cost to the province for maintenance of the foreign bam patients admitted during 1907, spread over the years they will he on our hands, will amount to the sum of $1,487,038.80 without taking into account tile compounding of interest, cost of buildings and many other items of expense which are sure to arise in the future.
Then he proceeds as follows :
Of the estimated total population of the province over sixteen years of age, 1,209,303 were Canadians and 291,675 foreigners, or twenty per cent of the whole. At the same time, of the commitments to jail thirty-eight per cent were of foreign birth and the cost of providing for them amounted to $21,724.65.
The difference in percentage is rather striking. The percentage of persons born outside of Canada committed to jail should be 20 per ceDt. Instead of that it is 38 per cent, or nearly double. That seems to me to indicate a rather serious condition of affairs. He goes on to say :
Toronto asylum gave a practical illustration of the position. Of 262 persons admitted less than half were Canadians.
I have obtained the exact figures. They are 134 born outside of Canada and 128

born in Canada, and among those 134 born outside of Canada, 77 were recent arrivals. Mr. Hanna continues :
Of course, many of the foreign born had been resident in Canada for some years, but no less than seventy-seven were recent arrivals, who should have been deported if a satisfactory law had been in force. The majority of these people should not have beeri allowed to enter Canada. Owing to technicalities, only twenty-four came within the requirements of the Deportation Act, and therefore Ontario had to assume the cost of maintaining forty-three. That meant that the province would have to expend $224,000 for the support of people who had not the slightest claim for their consideration. No matter how it was regarded, the picture was one that could not be contemplated with equanimity. The figui'es, he claimed, showed that the proportion of insane among arrivals was twenty-six times greater than it should be, and there was a strong suspicion that many were deliberatetly sent out from Great Britain to be got rid of. An analysis showed that whole families of degenerates were included among arrivals, and weaklings of all objectionable types were represented, as well as many with criminal records.
In a communication to me, Mr. Hanna says :
An analysis of their characteristics is an interesting study in degeneracy of a type we rarely see in Canada. Sexual perverts of the most revolting kind, the criminal insane, slum degenerates, general paretics, in fact weaklings of all objectionable types are represented. Whole families of degenerates have been found.
Under these circumstances, I do not think it can be contended that our inspection of these people is what it ought to be. Does the hon. Minister of the Interior or the hon. member for East Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) realize the care that Is taken in this regard in the Uuited States ? In that country they have created an expert department for the purpose of detecting mental infirmities. While I have several extraets on this subject, I will read only one. Dr. Salmon says :
At first thought it would seem a hopeless task to attempt to pick insane and mentally defective immigrants from the unending lines of humanity which file through Ellis Island, but a systematic plan of inspection has been devised which results in the dectection of many. Officers of the Public Health and Marine Hospital Service, who have had special training in institutions for the insane, are assigned to this duty, and the other medical officers unite with them in searching for immigrants who seem a typical or who present sivns even remotely suggesting mental disease.
Then he goes on to enumerate various other precautions taken for the purpose of detecting any mental infirmity.
I would like to make this one suggestion before I close. It does seem to me that we should have some regard to the fact that we have in Canada surely as good a Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
country for the immigrant, under present conditions, as can be found on the face of the globe. I have only to remind my hon. friends opposite, who want to discuss this question in a dispassionate manner and with the view of doing what is best in the interests of the country and of assuring ourselves that future generations will have nothing on account of which to reproach us in connection with our policy, that we have in the Northwest and the eastern provinces as well as lands to offer to the best races of the world which ought to induce the very best elements of their populations to come to this country. Look at the United States to-day. Let me quote the words of Mr. James J. Hill showing how little Is left in the United States for the emigrating races of Europe. In an address delivered on ' The Nation's Future ' at St. Paul, Minn, on the 3rd September, 1906, Mr. Hill spoke as follows :
The United States has been able easily to take care of the great increase of population in the past been use _it had a vast area of unoccupied land. This was the main asset in its natural inheritance. Within practically the last half of the last century the whole country from the Mississippi river to the Rocky mountains was occupied. No pressure of population could make itself severely felt when it might be turned loose in such an empire. In those fifty years there were added 547,640,932 acres to the agricultural area, an increase of nearly 200 per cent and the increase in the actually improved acreage was nearly 300 per cent. This is cut off from the list of resources. Within the last six years there have been transferred from public to private ownership more than 100,000,000 acres of government land, an area twice the size of the state of Minnesota, The entire area of surveyed and unappropriated land within the United States is only 2j times that amount.
At the present rate therefore every acre of public land would disappear within the next fifteen rears. But as a large percentage of the lands included in this estimate are wholly or partially unfit for tillage, it is literally true to say that our arable public lands have almost disappeared. And where are our children to find standing room and the tens of millions of the future a place for wholesome industry? This is an intensely practical question. It is immediate. For within twenty years we must house and employ m some fashion 50,000,000 of additional population; and by the middle^ of this century, at a time when the child now born will be in the prime of life, 'there will be approximately 21 times as many people in the United States as there are to-day.
With such a prospect of access of population to this great continent of which Canada forms a part, ought we to be in a hurry to bring into this country any except those who are the most desirable ? Therefore I repeat once more that it Is a question of quality and not of quantity to which the immigration policy of the government should in the future be directed. I do not minimize the necessity of the west for

population-the immediate necessity of the west-but with 215,000 people coining in withouf any bonus at all, surely we may say that the day of the bonus has gone by, and surely, with the reports of the asylums of Ontario before us, we ought to exercise a little more discretion regarding the fitness of these people than we have seen fit to use in the past. The strain of the blood of the people of Canada is a good one. It is one we are proud of. And it is no harm to say so because that man is not worth very much who is not proud of the race from which he has sprung and the blood which runs in his veins. The men who first came to this country, its pioneers, came from the shores of France, and the best blood of France from the peasant to the noble, was represented in that population which came to hew out homes for themselves in the wilderness three hundred years ago. After that we had the great trek of the Loyalists from the United States, at the time of the revolution, into Ontario and the maritime provinces and I believe also into the Eastern Townships. And when my hon. friend from South Perth (Mr. G. H. McIntyre) said no doubt inadvertently, that all our ancestors had come to this country for the purpose of bettering their condition, I would desire to take issue with him as regards that particular class. These men sacrificed home and propertv and prospects everything almost that men hold dear, in order that they might remain under that flag which floats to-day over Canada and proclaims Canada to be part of the British empire. And later on those who came from Scotland, Ireland, England and Germany as well-the pioneers of Ontario and Quebec and the maritime provinces-these people were surely of the best strain that the countries from which they came could give. They came to the wilderness and hewed out homes for themselves. They converted that which was a wilderness a hundred years ago into a garden. They were the makers of Canada, not only in the material but in every sense, and the history of these people, their energy, their courage, their devotion, their faith in the future of this country, should remain an imperishable memory in the hearts of every true Canadian. Therefore surely the parliament of this country should especially look to it to see that this strain of blood in every province shall be maintained without taint and without loss of the strength, vigour and vitality which we have maintained in Canada up to the present. I have detained the House longer than I intended, and shall only say in conclusion that I shall vote for the amendment of my hon. friend.

Although this debate has been protracted to a very great length, I am sure the time of the House has been very well
occupied. In fact I do not believe it has been so well occupied during the whole of this session. The subject brought to our attention is a very important one, and therefore it is important that it should be discussed in all its aspects and phases. If I may be permitted to express my own opinion, I think the debate has been maintained on a very high plane and does credit to the House. As regards the speech of my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk). I am bound to say that he put his views in a very able and on the whole a very moderate manner. But with all due deference to those views, he has failed, in my conception at all events, to appreciate the. true point of view-the only point of view from which this question can be approached and solved. The position taken by my hon. friend is that we should put an end to the policy of immigration we have been carrying out for many years. No doubt he will take issue with me on that point and say it is not his intention to put an end to the whole system; but although he does not say so in so many words, he wants to put an end to the salient feature of that system, without which it would be ineffective. He wants to put an end, I say, to that system of immigration, which, at last, has brought under cultivation those fertile lands of the west long dormant, long useless, but now, perhaps, the most important part of our national development. His opinion is that we should let nature unaided produce such results as it may; that we should, in a happy-go-lucky spirit, aw'ait and accept such results as chance may bring forth. The motive which has inspired him, so far as I have been able to appreciate it-for, I believe, on this point my hon. friend has not been as clear as in some other parts of his speech-is the fear that the present system w'hich wre have followed and are now following exposes us to the danger of having our population contaminated by certain undesirable elements. Well, Sir, the position I intend to take upon this question, the position to which I desire to draw the attention of the House, is that the primary aud dominant consideration which should influence every gentleman in this House and this country is to retain and maintain upon the soil of Canada every man who is born in Canada. And, Sir, it is a strange fact, it is a fact that it has only been by the impetus given to our national life through our policy of immigration that we have put an end to the scourge of emigration which, for years, was a running sore in the very vitals of our country. My hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) has spoken eloquently and w'ell of the devotion of those who, in the last years of the eighteenth century sacrificed everything that they might remain subjects of the British Crown, who left everything they had in the American colonies and came here to make

new homes for themselves in what was then a wilderness. The praise he gave to these people could not be too high. There never was, perhaps, in any part of the world, a greater example of devotion to conviction. But, Sir, it is a fact that the descendants of those men, and the descendants also of the early French pioneers who likewise came here from very similar motives to hew out for themselves homes in the forests of Canada-the descendants of these people at a certain time could not find a living in their own country, but went away by thousands and hundreds of thousands to seek homes in a foreign land no better endowed by nature than their own. Must I remind my hon. friends opposite that in the closing thirty, years of the last century, up to the taking of the last census, the population of Canada did not increase. Decade followed decade, census followed census, but every census had the same story to tell, that Canada hardly retained even its own native population. During all these years mothers brought forth children, but when the time came to enumerate them they were not to be found in the land. Our census showed that in 1891 the population of Canada was 4,883,239, the increase during the preceding decade having been only 5-9 per cent. At the end of the following decade in 1901, the population was 5.371.315, and during that decade the population had increased barely 11 per cent. And how was that 11 per cent made up ? British Columbia had increased 81 per cent. 

foreign population; Manitoba had increased 67 per cent-foreign population ; the Northwest Territories had increased 113 per cent-foreign population. And what were the increases in the older provinces ? In New Brunswick, barely 3 per cent; in Nova Scotia, barely 2 per cent; in Ontario, 3 per cent; in Prince Edward Island less than 1 per cent: in Quebec, 10 per cent. The same story had been told by the preceding census. During that decade, ending 1891, New Brunswick showed no increase; Nova Scotia, 2 per cent; Ontario, 9 per cent; Prince Edward Island less than 1 per cent; Quebec, 9 per cent. These figures show the condition of affairs down to 1901. Sir, it is written in the Book that the Angel of Death visited the land of the Egyptians and smote the first born. If any one, not knowing our history had taken the record of these two censuses, he would have believed that even a worse visitation had come upon us. that the Angel of Death had passed through our land aud smitten not only the first born but the whole offspring of the nation. These were not dead, but they were lost to us. They had gone, as I have said, from their own country to benefit and favour another with their presence and their labour.
Sir, in the history of the nineteenth century, there is perhaps no page more notable than that on which is recorded the extraor-Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
dinary development of the United States which brought its population from only two and a half millions, as it was at the time the constitution was adopted in 1789, to no less than 80.000 000 as it is to-day. What is the cause of this wonderful increase ? Undoubtedly, the first had been the glamour under which the new nation sprang into life. The appearance of this new democratic community amongst the monarchies of the world was an event that claimed the attention of the people of every country who had their own aspirations to freedom and who, not satisfied with their own laws, sought refuge in the new land. But it would be a fallacy to suppose that this first cause of immigration to the United States was not favoured and helped by the Americans themselves. My hon. friend the member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) stated a few days ago in proposing his motion that the Americans had made no effort to bring immigration into their midst. If he meant that the federal government had done nothing of that kind, he was right. But what was not done by the federal authority was done by the state government. I have only to quote to my hon. friend a book which is in the hands of everybody, the last edition of the ' Encyclopedia Americana.' In that work he will find the following:
The first legislation in the United States on the subject of immigration was of March 2, 1819, and merely provided that a record should be kept of the number of passengers arriving in each customs district, with their sex, age, occupation and country of birth. For many years there was no thought of anything but exultation in the number of arrivals, as increasing the wealth of the coun-trv and providing an asylum for the poor and oppressed. Even the Know-Nothink agitation of the fifties, prompted bv political reasons, led to no restrictive legislation. In 1864 the first Immigration Act was passed by Congress, and was to promote and not restrain it; this was repealed 1868. Several states established immigration bureaus to encourage it and draw it their way.
Not only was there this action on the part of several states of the union, but the railway companies likewise established bureaus in Europe to bring immigration their way in order to sell their lands and to create traffic for their systems. Navigation companies did likewise. There was a continuous procession of immigrants from all the countries of Europe into the United States. In that long procession the country which led the way was Ireland. For this immigration from Ireland there was not only the same cause which affected the rest of Europe, but, as we all know, the bad and vicious legislation of years was followed in Ireland by famine. One-half the population of Ireland passed over from that country to the United States. Next after Ireland, the country which stands second in the long procession, in propor-

tion to the number of its population, is Canada. In 1901, as I have just said, the population of Canada was 5,371,315. Of this number 4,671,815 were born in Canada, the rest were bom elsewhere. But in that same year the American census showed that of the American population 1,183,255 had been born in Canada. Therefore, \ye had at that moment of people born in Canada, and living either in Canada or in the United States, 5,855,070. Of this number every one in five had gone to the United States. What was the cause ? The cause is not difficult to find. The newcomers in the United States had to be fed and clothed and shod. They had to be supplied with tools, instruments, furniture, with all the requirements of modern civilization. A tremendous impetus was thus given to American industries. The labour market of the United States was a great attraction to our hardy population, who went to find in the United States the employment which their own country could not give them, and there, Sir, you have the explanation of the calamitous exodus which for so many years was a sore upon our country. Under these circumstances what was to be done? Were we to remain idle and make no effort to arrest this current of emigration? No, our policy was to tear a leaf out of the book of the Americans, and we not only tore a leaf out of the book of the Americans, but we went them one better. What the federal authorities at Washington left to the state governments, we did ourselves, and the results have been what we know them to be to-day, that immigration which had been coming in a thin and narrow stream, came at last in a copious flood, and not only was emigration from Canada to the United States stopped, but we now have an immigration from the United States to Canada.
Do not the American returns show that there were 19,918 emigrants from Canada to the United States last year?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Pardon me, the records of the United States do not show anything of the kind; they show that out of the immigration which came to Canada last year 19,000 immigrants percolated from Canada into the United States. But the records, so far as I have seen them, do not show that 19,000 native Canadians went to the United States. But, Sir. I do not care so much for statistics in this matter as I do for the horse sense of the people. Does not everybody know today that there is practically no emigration from Canada to the United States? Does not everybody now say that there is a stream of immigration from the LTnited States to Canada? Why, Sir, in the olden times when these gentlemen were in office, they used to pile up statistics mountains high to prove to ns that the country was
prosperous, but when the people put their hands into their pockets they could not find prosperity there. At the present time those hon. gentlemen are piling up figures mountains high to show that there is no prosperity in this country, but when the people put their hands into their pockets they find it there. It is no use for my hon. friend to quote statistics to prove that there is still a current of emigration from Canada to the United* States, because it does not exist, and everybody knows it.
Do you deny the correctness of the American statistics ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend is quoting American authorities. I will also quote from an American newspaper, the New York ' Sun.' which a few days ago published this article :
News comes from Winnipeg that the spring tide of emigration from our Western states to Canada has already set in and gives promise of reaching at least high water mark. This is a serious loss to the United States. Accepting, as we may, the Canadian statistics of immigration, it appears that since the opening of the century about 300,000 people have moved across the line to make homes in Canada. Probably a few have returned, but most have stayed and are content to stay.
These people do not go to Canada because they are not doing well in the United States, but because they hope to do better in the new land. Many of them are of the class which has made our great west. They or their fathers obtained lands in the west either by homesteading or by purchase for a small sum an acre. They can now sell their holdings for many times the original cost and take their money, their experience and their equipment into a new country, and there buy land for a few dollars an acre and see its value increase as did the value of their farms in this country.
Speaking in the Canadian House of Commons a few days ago, the Hon. Clifford Sifton said of these people:
I desire to say that I do not think any country conld possibly get a better class of settlers than the western Americans who have come into our western provinces. They are vigorous, resourceful, law abiding; they become citizens the day they arrive in the country, and at the earliest possible moment they become producers.
I am glad to see that this testimony of my hon. friend from Brandon (Mr. Sit'ton) is verified by the testimony of my bon. friend the leader of the opposition. This article goes on to say :
In point of numbers this exodus from our west to the Canadian west is in part offset by arrivals in onr eastern states from eastern Canada, but Canada gets muchlhe better end of the bargain in the exchange of population in both quality and quantity. Comparatively few Canadians now come to this country either for temporary work or for permanent residence, and many who came in earlier years have gone back, some to their former homes and many to new homes in the Northwest.

Many of these Canadian transients and many of the American emigrants take money with them. A considerable cash capital is not at all infrequent.
Was a bonus paid on them ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Well, I would like to know what my hon. friend wants to make out of that question. If he knows himself he will tell us ; for my part I do not understand him. Now, this is the result of our policy. I say, subject to contradiction, and I do not think I can be successfully contradicted, that our policy has put an end to the scourge of emigration. But now the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) comes forward and says. Halt, stop all this, reverse your policy. I answer the hon. member for Jacques Cartier, if we halt, if we reverse our policy, and revert to the old conditions which existed before this policy was adopted, what would be the result? Let me say here that this policy was not our own creation, it was not our own invention, it was the invention of hon. gentlemen of the Conservative party. They do not seem to be at all proud of it now, but it is their misfortune. Because it is successful now they do not want it, and they did want it when it was not successful. Why was it not successful? Because they never carried it out with a stout heart. They always administered it in a feeble manner, in such a feeble manner that at one time they thought seriously of putting an end to it. But there was at that time a man of resolute opinion, a man of strong courage, if there ever was a man who had courage, and the name of that man was Sir Charles Tupper. Sir Charles Tupper wishes the Canadian government of to-day to maintain this policy, and he has reason for it. I will not quote the letter which he sent to Mr. Carling, it has already been quoted by my hon. friend from East Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff).
Now, I shall give the House the opinion of a noted French economist as to what would be the effect of a cessation of immigration to this country. Mr. Anatole Le Roy-Beaulieu is one of the leading French economists of the present day. He wrote an article to apply not to this country but to the United States, but I quote it, as the condition is absolutely similar in Canada, to-show what would be the consequences of what is suggested by.hon. gentlemen opposite. Mr. Le Roy-Beaulieu contributes an article to ' La Revue Hedomadaire ' of January 4, 1908, upon American immigration, and this is what he says :
With a large number of Americans there exists, at present, an inclination, if not to prohibit, at least, to restrict immigration. Their present laws have already set an obstacle in its way; all who desire to land there may not do so. There are certain categories of people excluded-those stricken with con-Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
taoious diseases, idiots, anarchists, the indigent and those who threaten to become a menace or a burden for the commonwealth. Every immigrant should be possessed of ten dollars. This amount might be slightly raised; entrance might be made" more difficult; but it is not apparent that this would be a benefit to the United States. To diminish immigration would be to check the development of the population in the United States, and thereby shackle its economic impetus-for, it must not be lost sight of that, if the United States has had such a wonderful expansion in the world, it is due above all to immigration. It lias been proven that families, which have been American for four or five generations, are less prolific than are the families of immigrants. Consequently, it might well occur that, with the checking of immigration, the population might become stationary.
Who would benefit thereby? In the first place, Canada; possibly also Europe. But they who would above all benefit thereby are the Latin American states. They will possess vast expanses of territory calculated to form two or three republics such as the United States. It would greatly benefit Mexico, Brazil, the Argentine Republic, the Latin section and Latin civilization-all of which need scarcely more than a strong current of immigration to equal the United States in development. It may possibly happen that when the United States has two or three hundred millions of inhabitants, there may no longer exist there anv interest in securing emigrants from Europe. Moreover, it is questionable whether in fifty years, or in one hundred years, the European population will continue to increase as it does today and have as large a number of emigrants to forward to the shores of the other continent.
Be the future what it may, it now seems that, from both the standpoints of population and of industrial activity, the United States has every interest in not closing its doors against the newcomers from Europe.
Up to the present, it is true, not only has the United States freelv' received emigrants, but has quicklv naturalized them. Frequently they have been accorded the rights of American citizenship before they were able to exercise them. Therein lie abuses and mistakes from which the United States, from which at times the European peoples, might have to suffer; but the remedy is easy. All that is required would be to exact a longer sojourn on the part of the emigrants before granting them the rights of citizenship. For exemple, they might be accorded after a residence of twenty vears:_ a knowledge of the English language might be required of them. In a word, it would be easy to raise a barrier in the pathway of those strangers who unduly lay claim to such rights. To this I can see no serious objection. The Americans would gain thereby; equally so would the European countries; nossiblv even the emigrants themselves, for when they secure their rights of citizenship too easily they become the prey of politicians who dragoon them, who, for party and not for national interests, drive them to vote. Consequently, a title to American citizenship not being so freely granted, benefits wmuld arise for all-save the adventurers and political agitators.
This reservation as to the obtaining of

political franchise being excepted. I believe that the United States would commit a grave error in opposing any legal barriers to the emigrants from Europe. The United States has every interest, political and economic, in remaining, as heretofore, open to all white men who are sufficiently enterprising to brave the Atlantic. In the past century this has been one of the sources of American greatness, it is still so for the present, and will long remain so in the future.
This is intended for the American people but does not every word of it apply also to Canada ? If we check immigration to this country we thereby check our prosperity and we expose ourselves to the danger of reverting to the position in which we were ten years ago. Now, what Is the objection to this policy ? The objection which has been raised is not against the policy itself so much as against the possible consequences of the policy. It is that, possibly, if we maintain that system of encouraging immigration, we may bring in a certain number of undesirables and degenerates. My hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) insisted upon that at great length and he made some statements which rather gave me a shock. He stated that our surveillance was not as effective as that of the Americans, and that we accepted degenerates and undesirables. Our immigration laws are almost word for word in that respect the same as the American laws. But, the statement of my hon. friend, or the impression that he gave was that the surveillance of the Americans was much more severe and exacting than ours and that ours was very lax. He also made the statement that we allowed in certain parties who, upon seeking admission to the United States, were rejected as undesirables. My hon. friend, as I said a moment ago, made certain statements that gave me a shock and I thought I would investigate the matter for myself I will give the result of my investigation, but perhaps I cannot do better than give the very words of my hon. friend in order that I may not misquote him or be unfair to him. This is what he said on that question on the occasion to which I have reference :
Of those arriving at Canadian ports with the avowed and declared intention of going to the .United States there were 12,663 and 183 were debarred. What became of them when they were debarred at our Canadian ports I do not know, it is impossible to find anv trace of their disposition. Were they sent back to Europe in the vessels in which they came to Canada? I doubt it very much. If, on the contrary they did not land and proceeded without examination to one of the examining stations on the Canadian frontier and were there debarred, I doubt very much if they were deported back to Europe.
The second class are those destined to Canada and who have gone to the United States within a year after their arrival in this country. They have to submit to examination at one of the numerous examining stations which the United States government have established along the border, on the ground that we admitted a great manv undesirables who found their wav into the United States. After having made representations to the Canadian government on that subject which to a large extent the American commissioners admit have been carried out, still they have found it necessary to establish these posts of examination. In the second class of immigrants we find 8,517 and 589 were debarred. I shall not go into the details of the causes of their exclusion from the United States, many were refused admission for those causes which were causes of exclusion from Canada and hoiv they succeeded in entering Canada I do not know. Nor do I know what became of them when they were refused admission to the United States. It is impossible to trace the matter any further, but my own view is that they remained in Canada, and that we have to-day in Canada these immigrants who were deemed undesirables under the American law for pronounced and stated causes.
Nothing can be clearer than that my hon. friend conveyed the impression that while the Canadian authorities at Quebec had allowed a certain number to come in of an undesirable character these parties, upon seeking admission to the United States, were turned back and they had remained in our midst ever since. My hon. friend professed to be very much aggrieved by that state of affairs. My hon. friend and I are old friends and I would not leave him in an agony of doubt. My hon. friend is pained and chagrined to believe that there are hundreds and perhaps thousands of degenerates who have sought admission to the United States but who were kept in this country. But if the hon. gentleman had looked further into the report of the American commissioner from which he quoted he would have been relieved of his pain ; be would have found there that according to the report of the American agent these degenerates have been sent back to Europe by the Canadian authorities. This is what I find in the report of the American commissioner, and if my hon. friend had examined it more carefully it is there for him to also find it.
Notwithstanding the fact that the bureau of immigration was duly represented at all the Atlantic ocean ports of the Dominion of Canada by a commissioner and a full corps of inspectors as early as 1893, no deportations whatever are recorded prior to the above mentioned date, (September 1, 1901) so that the whole value of accomplished results up to that time was lost, firstly for want of a sufficient border force, and secondly because the Dominion of Canada made no scrutiny of its immigrants, and consequently had not made arrangements, at least in practice, for deporting undesirables.
Now, however, a change has been effected, a most salutory one, in both instances, the United States has strongly guarded the border at all its vulnerable points, and the Dominion government finding the unwelcome stream



successfully dammed and flowing back on itself, bas made very rapid strides towards adopting a policy, in the main similar to the bureau's policy.
As an evidence of this change, it should be stated that the Canadian immigration department has deported a large number of applicants for admission to Canada on the ground that they were unfit to mingle with the citizens of Canada in the pursuit of that life and pleasure which they came here to find.
Not only has Canada deported large numbers of undesirables, who sought to permanently settle in Canada, but of the 24,797 applicants for permission to pass through Canada to the United States, those who were rejected by your officers as unfit persons under United States laws, because of being afflicted with loathsome contagious diseases, were deported to Europe by the Dominion immigration authorities, the steamship companies bringing them to Canada being compelled to return them and to assume all expenses incident thereto.

This surely could not apply to the immigrants who have come from *Europe and who have been admitted to Canada by our own authorities and who within a year or after a year at one of the border stations tried to get into the United States and are refused. We could not deal with them because we have admitted them into this country.
How do you know ?

I know because there is no doubt about it. What the right hon. gentleman has said may perhaps apply to the immigrant when he arrives in Halifax or at the first port of landing in America, but it cannot apply to the other two classes I refer to, namely, the immigrant who is admitted to Canada by our own authorities and who is refused at Niagara or some other border station within a year or after a year.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
In the observation of my hon. friend there is both an admission and a negation and I will deal with the admission first. He may have said to-day that this report of the American agent applies, as it does apply, to those who land in Quebec intending to go to the United States, but what my hon. friend did say the other day was :
Of those arriving at Canadian ports with the avowed and declared intention of going to the United States there were 12,663 and 183 were debarred. What became of them when they were debarred at our Canadian ports I do not know, it is impossible to find any trace of their disposition. Were they sent back to Europe in the vessels in which they came to Canada? I doubt it very much.
* The hon. gentleman doubted it a few days ago but he does not doubt it now.
There is no proof of it in our own reports on immigration.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
There is a proof of it in the report of the American commis-Sir WILFRID LAURIEP
sioner from which my hon. friend was quoting. I shall read the words again.
What page V

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Page 79.
What report ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The report of 1904 which was quoted by my hon. friend (Mr. Monk). There is there a statement that those who are undesirable under American laws and landed at Quebec were sent back to Europe. This is what the American commissioner says :
Not only has Canada deported large numbers of undesirables, who sought to permanently settle in Canada, but of the 24,797 applicants for permission to pass through Canada to the United States, those who were rejected by your officers as unfit persons under United States laws, because of being afflicted with loathsome contagious diseases, were deported to Europe by the Dominion immigration authorities, the steamship companies bringing them to Canada being compelled to return them and to assume all expenses incident thereto.
Nothing could be plainer than this. Even on the admission of my hon. friend (Mr. Monk) this applies to those who landed in Quebec with the intention of going to the United States. The hon. gentleman asks : What becomes of those who resided in Canada for some time and then sought admission to the United States? Well, as I understand this report-but as to this I do not speak with the same certainty as with regard to the other question-as I understand this report those people were also examined at the border station and sent back because the American agent here speaks of 24,797 applicants for permission to pass through Canada to the United States and at page 87 of the report I find :
-	No. manifest- ed.	No. admitted.	No. rejected.E xamined at ocean * ports of arrival,.	15,399	15,097	262Examined by border boards of special inquiry..	9,438	8,771	667-and it gives the total manifested at 24,797 which is the same number mentioned by the commissioner in his report when he says :	_
But of the 24,797 applicants for permission to pass through Canada to the United States, those who were rejected by your officers as unfit persons under United States laws, because of being afflicted with loathsome contagious diseases were deported to Europe by the Dominion immigration authorities, the steamship companies bringing them to Can-

ada being compelled to return them and to assume all expenses incident thereto.
Therefore it shows as I understand it, that although they came later on they were examined at the border stations and rejected and sent hack to Europe. If that be so it is a complete answer to my hon. friend. But even if it were not so, are we to reject a system of this kind because there may be abuses under it. If my hon. friend were logical his conclusion would be that if the Americans have a superior system of examination we should adopt their system of examination but not reject their policy. Now, to deal with the remarks of the leader of the opposition ; he stated and stated correctly that many degenerates from England have been brought into Canada. But, Sir, far from that being a part of our system of immigration it is absolutely against our system, and we are doing our best to prevent these degenerates from landing in Canada. We know that charitable institutions are disposed to send such people out here, but we have protested against it and the Minister of the Interior in order to prevent a practice has issued an order in these words :
The minister, therefore, recommends that an order in council be passed prohibiting from and after the fifteenth day of April, 1908, the landing in Canada of any person whose passage has been paid, wholly or in part, by any charitable organization or out of public moneys unless it is shown that the authority in. writing of the assistant superintendent of emigration for Canada in London, has been obtained for the emigration of such person, and that such authority has been acted upon within a period of sixty days.
This regulation will it is expected absolutely do away with the practice which has prevailed in this respect. There is another feature of this question as to which I shall say a word. My hon. friend from Mont-magny (Mr. Lavergne) and my hon. friend from ' Quebec (Mr. Robitaille) have complained that we have no emigration system in France. But before I refer to that let me say to my hon. friend from Montma-gny that he made a statement in his speech which on reflection he seriously should regret, because it is absolutely unfair to a gentleman who is not in this House to defend himself, and for whose alleged action my hon. friend has sought to make the Canadian government responsible.
My hon. friend in his speech the other day wanted to prove that Mr. Smart had intended to devise a system specially against French immigration, and bethought he would support his contention by an extract from a newspaper which he had quoted last year. The extract is as follows :
The ' Northern Express,' Liverpool, February 10, 1902.-British blood is needed.

Smart, Deputy Minister of 2251
the Interior of Canada, and Mr. W. T. R. Preston, immigration agent general for the Dominion, arrived in Liverpool to-day from London and Glasgow to arrange a gigantic system of British immigration to Canada.
More British blood is also needed to be infused if the views of the Dominion of Canada is not to be Frenchified by the rapid growth of the French population.
Now, Sir, I ask my hon. friend, as a fair and candid man, where does he find that Mr. Smart used that language.
It is a mistake in 'Hansard'; the last words are the words used by Mr. Smart.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I have looked at my hon. friend's language in ' Hansard ' of last year, and it is exactly the same.
Yes, because I had the paragraph saying that Mr. Smart had said so and so, but I did not put in any notes. Only his words in ' Hansard ' are copied exactly.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I have not the paper at hand. I can only tell my hon. friend that if this is all the authority he has for accusing Mr. Smart, he is guilty of a serious and unwarranted accusation against an honourable man. First of all, is it fair or right? This is said to be an act in 1903. Mr. Smart has not been in the service of the government for four years. The attention of the government was never called to anything of the kind.
I beg the right hon. gentleman's pardon. It was called to their attention by the ex-member for Labelle, Mr. Bourassa.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: When?
At the time the statement was made, in 1902.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I never heard of it. I do not say that it was not done, but my attention was not called to it. If it had been, I would have thought it advisable to have called Mr. Smart's attention to it. But to say that we are responsible when Mr. Smart has not been in the employ of the government for four years is stretching our responsibility to an extreme point.
But now I come to the statement of my hon. friend from Montmagny that we have no system of immigration in France. I say at once that our system of immigration in France has been inadequate ; but we have had no better system there because we have had no direct line of communication between Canada and France. The government has made efforts for twenty years to establish such a line, not only for commercial purposes but for purposes of immigration. The moment we established a line of communication with France we

attempted to establish a system of immigration in France, and at present we have four immigration agents in that country- Mr. Wiallard, Mr. Foursin, Mr. Geoffrion and Mr. Montpetit. In addition to these we have sent from time to time different agents. H. F. Morel was appointed as delegate to Belgium for four months from December 7, 1907. Mr. Morel already has had experience at this work, having been employed for six months by the department as special agent from December, 1905, to June, 1906. Paul Auve, Morinville, Alberta, has been offered a position as farmer delegate in France. The department is not yet advised of his acceptance. He is a practical farmer and has spent fifteen years in western Canada. J. E. Des-lauriers has been appointed temporarily to do emigration work in France and Belgium. He would probably enter upon his work on or about the 1st instant. Edouard Parent, of St. Jean Baptiste, Manitoba, had been appointed as farmer delegate to France. The appointment is for three months from January 20, 1908. Mr. Parent is a qualified farmer and strongly recommended as a suitable man.
Now that we have a line of communication with France, we will pursue the work with all possible diligence, because we realize-and in this I am sure I voice the sentiments of everybody in this House and out of it-that we cannot have a more valuable class of immigrants than the French peasants and the Belgian peasants. Every one acknowledges that they possess thrift, morality and all the qualities that go to make good citizens. For these reasons I think my hon. friend will exempt us from the blame he has attempted to fasten upon us.
Now, I have only one word more to say. Everybody admits that one of the sources of wealth of any. nation is its immigration. All economists agree that the immigrant brings with him a source of wealth, not only in the cash which he possesses but in the labour he brings to the country of his adoption. The value of the wealth which an immigrant brings to a country has been variously estimated; it is impossible to give an exact figure in that respect. Some have estimated the value at $1,000; but this is not very satisfactory. I find in an American work on immigration by Prescott F. Hall, a paragraph which sems to give a fairly satisfactory basis of estimating the value of an immigrant. Mr. Hall says :
It is difficult, therefore, to say precisely what the money value of the immigrant is. The remote as well as the immediate effects of his coming must be considered, and also the state of employment and the rate of wages at the time of hip arrival. A thoroughly conservative estimate is probably that of Mr. John B. Webber, formerly Commissioner of Immigration at the port of New York. He assumes that there were 10,000,000 foreign born at the date of the eleventh Sir WILFRID LAUBIER
census and that 2,000.000 of these were working at an average of $1 per day; and he points out that these persons added $600,000,000 a year to the earnings of the country.
Now, Sir, last year we received over 200,000 immigrants. If we take the estimate of Mr. Hall that twenty per cent of these were earning $1 a day, these immigrants added to the wealth of the country no less than $12,000,000. We know for a fact that the American immigrants brought into the country, in money and goods equivalent to money, in one year $49,000,000 and in another year over $50,000,000. Does anybody think under such circumstances that we should deprive ourselves of the valuable addition to our wealth which our policy of immigration has brought to this country ? Sir, if we were to do that, we would revert to the condition of ten years ago when we were losing our population. I do not claim that the policy we have at the present time is to be permanent ; it is only a temporary policy ; it cannot last for ever ; but under the existing circumstances, with a powerful neighbour to the south, having a population of 80,000,000, while our population is only 6,000,000, the time has not yet some for departing from that policy, and I would therefore invite the House to reject the motion of my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier.

This House regrets that the sums spent by the country to pay bonuses on immigration have not been employed in bringing back to our country the Canadians who hare emigrated to the United States.
